  • Recent findings suggest that A whistle blew.
  • In a recent development, when I got out of the pool, I walked over to my kids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Twenty-four years. That’s how long it had been since I last stood atop a swim block, preparing to dive in for a timed race in an official meet.

Recent findings suggest that A whistle blew. The crowd hushed to silence. A monotone call came over the loudspeaker, “Swimmers, take your mark,” followed by a loud electronic beep that signaled the start of the race. I felt the cold rush of water overtake my body upon diving in. The neurons in my brain feverishly told my muscles to complete the strokes I’d learned decades before. In seconds, it was done. I finished the race.

In a recent development, when I got out of the pool, I walked over to my kids. My son, a competitive swimmer himself, looked at me and earnestly mentioned, “Wow, Mom. I’m proud of you.”.

In a recent development, like most moms, I have a packed schedule. I work, parent, volunteer at school, shepherd my two kids to practices and social gatherings, throw meals together, walk the dog, and occasionally find a moment to breathe. But over the past couple of years, I watched my growing kids, now ages 12 and 9, discover and engage in passions that light them up. It left me wondering, why not me, too?

“A recurring theme in my practice is women feeling they’ve lost their individual identities somewhere between work, parenting, and meeting everyone else’s needs,” notes Carly Snyder, a Upcoming York City–based reproductive and perinatal psychiatrist. “Part of my work involves helping women recognize that their own interests and needs are legitimate.”.

Sources indicate that research highlights a multitude of benefits earned by pursuing hobbies. Hobbyists often have wider social networks, improved mental health markers, and enhanced positive emotions.

Hobbies offer a particularly vital lifeline for mothers, who often report losing themselves to the demanding needs of family life. That rings true for Kaitlyn Edington, an art educator and mom of two who recalls struggling after returning to work as a teacher following the birth of her first child. “I was so depleted,” Edington says. She spent her workdays teaching with short breaks to pump, often bringing her computer into her pumping room so she could catch up on work, then went home to full nights of infant care.

One day while scrolling on Instagram, Edington saw an artist posting images of her sketchbook paintings. “She changed my life,” Edington notes. “Her sketchbook paintings were so loose and free, and she was encouraging people to draw everyday. I remember thinking, ‘If I have to pump two to three times a day, which I absolutely hate, why not pair it with something that I love?’” From then on, Edington sketched when she pumped, and ultimately developed a habit of daily sketching that she continues 10 years later.

No longer in the pumping phase of life, Edington ensures she gets time to sketch by waking up before her kids. “I hold the habit of waking up before my kids as sacred,” she says. “I need that time, when nobody needs me. It’s my emotional rest.”.

In a recent development, science backs Edington’s belief that her hobby stabilizes her mental health. “Reengaging in meaningful, enjoyable activities can be therapeutically valuable,” Snyder indicates. “Behavioral activation, an evidence-based treatment for depression, specifically emphasizes reconnecting with activities that provide pleasure, purpose, or a sense of accomplishment.”.

According to recent reports, snyder has three children, ages 19, 16, and 11, and throughout their lives she has maintained her dedication to skiing, cycling, yoga and running, completing a total of 19 marathons. She knows her kids benefit from her hobbies. Each time Snyder trains for an upcoming marathon, “[My kids] witness my commitment, discipline, setbacks, and perseverance,” she states. “Watching a parent pursue a hobby provides opportunities to observe persistence, emotional regulation, problem-solving, and enjoyment.”.

But those benefits are secondary to the impacts hobbies have on the women pursuing them. “I think we’ve become so accustomed to framing everything mothers do in terms of how it benefits their children,” Snyder says. “Women are entitled to happiness and fulfillment for their own sake.”.

Industry observers note that it’s simply an added bonus that when mom is happy for mom’s sake, the benefits for her kids naturally follow, according to multiple studies linking a mother’s well-being with her child’s. Plus, kids also learn that all stages of adulthood, including those under the umbrella of parenting, can include personal fulfillment, curiosity, and growth.

The best way to start a hobby is to let yourself reconnect with something you already love. I remembered how much joy I got out of competing in swim meets in high school, and I was eager to recreate that glee. Ask yourself, “What did I love when I was a kid or a young adult?”.

Your hobby doesn’t have to involve intense commitment. “Reading, gardening, dancing, listening to music, or simply spending time alone can be just as meaningful as running a marathon,” Snyder says.

According to recent reports, search online for local groups involved in the activity you want to pursue. Your local library may have resources to help you get started as well.

When you’re ready to commit, set realistic goals. Start by focusing on your hobby consistently for just 10-15 minutes per day. Showing up is the main goal.

Industry observers note that “Motherhood should expand a woman’s identity, not erase it,” Snyder advises. Which hobby will help expand yours?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I don’t care if I’m reliant on it and you can’t make me.

Recent findings suggest that sleep deprivation is a form of torture. At some point in every adult’s life, you find out why the hard way. Every parent goes through intense sleep deprivation when they bring home their first baby, and every subsequent newborn after that. But for some of us, sleep never came easy. By the time the babies came on the scene, we were well acquainted with the wee hours of the morning, what it felt like to be up all night, every night.

As a kid, I remember lying in bed for long stretches of time before I could fall asleep. My thoughts would race about everything and nothing. I had a dream catcher above my bed to ward off nightmares, worry dolls under my pillow to whisper my anxieties to so they could “hold them for me” until the morning, and my bedroom TV volume on low while a plucky Disney Channel show played. At sleepovers I was always the last to fall asleep, if I managed to stay overnight at all.

Recent findings suggest that I didn’t get a formal anxiety diagnosis until I went off to college many years later, but learning more about my brain finally gave me an understanding of why sleep was so elusive. With a nervous system stuck in fight-or-flight mode, of course I’d wake at the slightest sound and have a nearly impossible time winding down enough to knock out at the end of the day.

Finally, in 2019, I expressed my frustrations to my upcoming psychiatrist. I was awake for hours every night waiting for sleep to come, while my husband was already in REM before he ever got fully horizontal on the mattress. I tried guided meditations (why do all the beach ones feature squawking seagulls?) and binaural beats and exercising with the goal of exhausting myself during the day, but my insomnia had reached a frustrating new intensity. It was making my anxiety and depression so much worse; I looked and felt utterly bedraggled. So, he prescribed me trazodone.

While trazodone isn’t a true sedative — it’s actually an antidepressant — it’s often used off-label to treat insomnia because it gives you a similar relaxing, drowsy feeling. My doctor told me that it’s not a controlled substance and carries a very low risk of addiction, but that mentally, I might start to feel like I need it in order to sleep. If I didn’t like feeling dependent on it, we could make some changes.

“Are they going to stop making it any time soon?” I asked.

“Is it bad to take long-term for any other reason?”.

“Then I’m perfectly fine with being mentally addicted,” I stated. And I’ve taken it every single night since then.

According to recent reports, research has shown again and again that regularly sleeping well is a key quality-of-life indicator. Lack of sleep negatively impacts every system of the body, weakening the immune system, worsening mental health, and increasing risk of countless conditions, from high cholesterol to Alzheimer’s. Women are twice as likely to have insomnia as men, which has been attributed to our natural hormonal fluctuations throughout the month and the fact that we tend to carry the lion’s share of the mental load in the family, on top of being more prone to mood disorders.

In a recent development, yet even though we know all of this, taking anything to help you fall asleep is still... kind of frowned upon. Researchers in the UK conducted focus groups interviewing people who take prescription sleep medications and OTC supplements, like melatonin, and found that they had a lot of internalized stigma around the subject — even when talking about it in a room full of people who also take something to help them sleep.

They found that participants were very deliberate in how they explained their need for their meds. They’re deserving (explaining that their condition, like chronic pain or anxiety, makes sleep impossible without medication). They’re compliant, only ever taking their meds exactly as prescribed (or, in the case of supplements, as directed on the label). They’re responsible, always watching themselves for signs of addiction or misuse. They expressed extreme guilt over taking more of their medications than they should, or trying alternative medications meant to make them sleepy when their usual prescription wasn’t enough.

We recently asked Scary Mommy’s Instagram followers the question, “Do you take anything to fall asleep at night?” Some of that same stigma indicated up in their responses too.

Multiple readers noted they take Gravol when they can’t sleep, calling it a “horrid habit” or something they only do “when things get really bad.” Another said, “I can’t sleep without a quarter of an Ambien. It’s terrible!” “Haven’t had an unmedicated sleep in 7+ years 🫠,” said one response. The melting face is doing a lot of heavy lifting there.

Industry observers note that of course there were plenty of Scary Mommies who felt no shame (that’s sort of our shtick around here). In response to the question “Do you take anything to fall asleep?” one user simply replied, “WINE.” Plenty of other respondents also take trazodone, or Unisom, or some other sleep aid. Weed, whether in vape or gummy form, is also an extremely popular option. See also: a large number of replies indicating they take magnesium and progesterone at night thanks to perimenopause, and that HRT was finally the thing to help them sleep through the night.

But one response really captures my feelings about the whole subject:.

Recent findings suggest that “Oh lord I’m so medicated. But it’s working.”.

Even on the days I feel like I shouldn’t have to take something to help me sleep, that perhaps I could sleepmaxx or wellness hack my way out of having to take a pill every night, I remind myself that not getting enough sleep is literally deadly.

When you’re someone who struggles with sleep night after night, you know how promptly your mental and physical health can plummet. Insomnia decimates my quality of life. Sleep deprivation locks my personality and my joy away behind a concrete wall where I can’t access them anymore. It impacts my longevity and my relationships. While I’m not saying every reader who responded has a healthy way of getting to sleep at night, or that we shouldn’t be critical of our relationships with substances, I think we could all use a little validation that not getting enough sleep is, in fact, torturous.

More moms need to hear that they deserve to sleep well. They should know that their doctors want to hear from them if they feel abnormally tired during the day. And I want more women to internalize the idea that this world is hard enough to live in as it is. You should at least be able to meet it each day not feeling like a shell of yourself.

And that’s why you can pry my trazodone out of my cold, dead hands.

250 Turkish Baby Names Inspired by Nature, Strength and Beauty

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Discover the beauty, meaning, and cultural stories behind 250 captivating Turkish names.
  • Have you ever met someone and immediately thought, Of course that’s their name?
  • Maybe their name sounds soft and peaceful, and that is exactly how they carry themselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Discover the beauty, meaning, and cultural stories behind 250 captivating Turkish names.

Have you ever met someone and immediately thought, Of course that’s their name?

Maybe their name sounds soft and peaceful, and that is exactly how they carry themselves. Perhaps it feels bold and powerful, matching their confidence before they have even mentioned a word. It can make you wonder how parents choose the perfect name for a baby they have only just met, and how they somehow know which name will grow to suit them.

Choosing a name often means imagining who that baby might become. Parents may be drawn to a particular meaning, family tradition or simply the way a name sounds, hoping it will feel right both in the first moments of life and many years later.

Industry observers note that names become part of how we understand people. Over time, they collect memories, personality traits, family stories and emotions. A name chosen for a newborn may begin with a meaning, a tradition or simply a beautiful sound, but it eventually becomes inseparable from the person carrying it.

Names can carry the same meaning and still sound completely different from one language to another. A name inspired by the moon may feel soft and luminous in one culture, yet bold, mysterious or quietly powerful in another.

It has been revealed that turkish names are especially rich in imagery. Many draw from the sky, the sea, the seasons and the natural world, turning a single word into something vivid and memorable. Aylin evokes a halo around the moon, Deniz and Derya call to mind the sea, Gunes means sun and Yildiz means star.

Others reflect qualities parents may hope their children will carry through life. Eren is associated with wisdom, Mert with bravery and honesty, and Umut with hope.

With roots in Turkic, Arabic, Persian and neighboring traditions, names used in Türkiye reflect a layered cultural history shaped by poetry, nature and generations of meaning.

According to recent reports, below are 100 names commonly used in Türkiye, presented in alphabetical order. The list includes feminine, masculine and gender-neutral options.

Akin – warrior or one who advances.

Alara – water fairy or mythic river spirit.

Arda – successor or one who follows.

Atalay – celebrated or renowned.

Ayaz – frost or cool, clear air.

Aysun – as beautiful as the moon.

Cagdas – contemporary or modern.

Candan – sincerely or from the heart.

Ceyda – graceful or beautiful woman.

Dilara – one who delights the heart.

Ebru – marbled pattern or cloudlike design.

Egemen – sovereign or independent.

Ekim – October or sowing season.

Ekin – harvest or cultivated field.

Elvan – colorful or multicolored.

Emine – trustworthy or faithful.

Emre – friend or loving companion.

Eren – wise or spiritually mature.

Erkan – noble or courageous man.

Esra – swift or nighttime traveler.

Evrim – evolution or transformation.

Gokce – heavenly or sky-colored.

Gurkan – strong or proud lineage.

Kamuran – fortunate or successful.

Koray – glowing or ember-colored moon.

Mine – enamel or delicate ornament.

Oguz – strong or historic Turkic tribe.

Omer – flourishing or long-lived.

Orhan – great ruler or army leader.

Sila – reunion with one’s homeland.

Tarkan – warrior or noble title.

Yaren – close friend or companion.

Zumra – emerald or precious stone.

Breaking: 29 Gifts For Moms Whose Favorite Form Of Therapy Is Travel

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that jSome clichés are clichés for a reason.
  • Recent findings suggest that so, when it comes to gifts you can give the moms in your life, it’s hard to beat travel gifts...
  • Here are some of our favorite travel-forward finds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can never go wrong with travel gifts, TBH.

Industry observers note that jSome clichés are clichés for a reason. Being a mom is really hard. But it’s so, so rewarding. Also, travel is the best teacher. For many moms, those three clichés are often true in tandem. Sometimes, the lessons we learn during travel make the invisible load of motherhood a little lighter to bear. Sometimes, the lesson is simply that we have to make time for ourselves to be the best moms we can be. And sometimes, seeing the world through our kids’ eyes is enough to remind us that even when the road is rough, the reward is usually worth it.

Recent findings suggest that so, when it comes to gifts you can give the moms in your life, it’s hard to beat travel gifts... especially when travel already seems to be their favorite form of therapy. While splurging on things as pricey as plane tickets or an all-inclusive resort stay is (understandably) out of reach for many of us, there are tons of items any travel-loving mom would be overjoyed to get. We should know! The Scary Mommy editors are all busy moms who enjoy squeezing getaways and adventures into whatever little pockets of spare time we can find.

Here are some of our favorite travel-forward finds.

In a recent development, I have the full-size Naturepedic pillow, and I yearn to own the travel-sized one too. I have chronic neck pain and headaches, so I need a soft yet supportive pillow and one that is comfortable when sleeping on my back or my side. I’ve purchased and used so many pillows in my day, and this is finally THE ONE. I love that you can customize how much stuffing you keep inside, and I like to form mine with a little divot for my head to maximize my neck support. The full-size is heavy, though, so I really want to find a travel-sized one under the tree this year to use instead of the down (deeply unsupportive) hotel pillows that leave me hurting. — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

This is the diaper bag I wish I’d had for every family trip with little ones! It fits a pump, bottles, diapers, a laptop... really, you’d be surprised how much stuff you can stuff in it. I especially love that there’s a quick-grab pocket on the front sized perfectly for wipes. Even though my kids are teens, I carry this as a carry-on backpack because it’s so pretty and functional, and it slips right over your suitcase handle so you have one less thing to juggle at the gate. Thanks to the easy-clean neoprene and chic design, it doesn’t scream “diaper bag.” — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

The Cincha Go-Tote has become my most-reached-for travel bag because it solves the one problem every traveler has: The carry-on that tips over every time you let go of it. The Cincha Go-Tote has a built-in luggage sleeve that slides right over your suitcase handle so everything stays put, and your hands stay free; plus it is water-resistant, has leather accents that make it look way more elevated than a travel bag has any right to look, and fits everything you need for a flight without becoming a black hole. This is for the traveler on your holiday list who has everything but still somehow does not have this. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

I have bought my fair share of travel pillows over the years, and a lot of them just... don't get the job done. I love this one because it stuffs into a small sack and it really does help you nod off on the plane without choking or smothering you. When I travel with this, people always ask me where it's from. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

I think my fresh favorite obsession is traveling with a trunk! For those trips when you need the extra space, this beauty lets you travel in style. It has such a sophisticated vintage-inspired look... it feels like it should be loaded onto the Orient Express. That old-world glamour even extends to a sleek double-latch closure (instead of a zipper) with TSA-approved locks. She’s not just pretty, though; she’s durable too, thanks to a tough polycarbonate shell, reinforced corners, and replaceable wheels. And once you get used to traveling trunk-style with its super-convenient deep side, it’ll be hard to go back! — Julie Sprankles.

Sources indicate that packing for a trip with kids usually means digging through a black hole for one sock, and these clear, color-coded organizers fix that. The set of four comes in substantial, medium, and mini sizes with windows so you can see exactly what’s inside, and my favorite part is that each one gets its own job, like clothes, snacks, or tech and first aid. They’re the unglamorous travel upgrade that makes packing and unpacking take minutes instead of hours, and I’m never traveling without them again!— Katie Garrity.

I don't know how many times I've had a fully charged battery back with me while traveling, but I can't find the right cord to attach it to my phone. This magnetic charger is small, mighty, and charges cordlessly! It has become my number one charging brick, and that indicates a lot coming from me. This is one of those products where you buy one and then almost immediately buy another one, just to have a spare. I also love getting these as gifts for people! — Sarah Aswell.

My non-negotiable for travel days is comfort, but I don’t want to look like I rolled right out of bed and onto the plane, either. These Cozy Earth joggers are just the ticket. They’re ridiculously soft, with a slim-but-relaxed fit and an adjustable drawstring that’s perfect for long flights. And the burgundy color is seriously stunning, so I look put-together even though I feel like I’m in my comfiest PJs. — Julie Sprankles.

Ask anyone who knows me, and they'll tell you my happy place is sitting out in the sun — wherever that may be. As someone who has long loved Gray Malin's art (but not someone who has been able to splurge on it as often as I'd like), these travel pouches make a great happy medium. I love how packable and useful these travel pouches are, but what I love most about them is how "in the mood" they'll get you to travel. As you pack up your stuff, you can practically taste vacation. What's not to love? — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief.

According to recent reports, for the traveler on your list who is still hauling around a beat-up suitcase, this is the upgrade that will make them feel like a seasoned jet-setter, with a slim aluminum frame and polycarbonate shell that look as sleek as they are tough. The 77-liter interior has a built-in compression panel for squeezing in just a little more and about 1.5 inches of extra depth, which is exactly what you need for a 7- to 10-day trip. It also has 360° spinner wheels and two TSA-approved locks, so it’s the gift that makes every airport trip a little less stressful! — Katie Garrity.

Like many people entering their 40s after a lifetime of wear and tear, I deal with a lot of foot complications, especially when I'm walking 20,000 steps a day while traveling. I love these shoe inserts that have gotten me through the most epic travel days, including 12-mile days at Disney World and a 15-mile day hike in Glacier National Park. — Sarah Aswell.

According to recent reports, while experts generally agree that airlines don’t reuse blankets, it’s still comforting just to carry your own on board. As someone who is always cold, I can’t tell you how much I appreciate being able to toss this into my carry-on. It comes with a super-soft throw, a matching eye mask, and the coordinating bag to stash them both in. — Julie Sprankles.

Recent findings suggest that this is the carry-on to match all carry-ons! This backpack opens super wide at the top so you can find anything you need, plus it has a large front zippered pocket for chargers, snacks, or notes from admirers. It fits so much stuff and yet still somehow slides perfectly under an airplane seat like some kind of backpack sorcery. — Katie Garrity.

Industry observers note that it’s just designed to fit so much more, even though it takes up the same amount of space as other bags. Used with the packing cubes from the same organization, I can easily fit a week’s worth of stuff into a bag and not have to check anything. — Sarah Aswell.

Marshall is such an iconic brand that I feel a little cooler every time I slip these headphones on. There are lots of reasons they’re great for tossing in your carry-on. The adaptive noise cancellation automatically blocks out plane noises, but one push of a button switches to transparency mode so I can hear flight announcements. The battery lasts up to 50-plus hours with ANC on. And, one of my favorite features, they’re made to fold up small so you can stash them in your bag without a hassle. — Julie Sprankles.

Recent findings suggest that this tote organizer turns any bottomless pit of a bag into an orderly dream. With pockets and pouches for all of your on-the-go essentials, the ToteSavvy makes traveling a breeze. — Katie Garrity.

S'well makes my favorite lunch salad bowl container; it never leaks and is super high-quality. So when I saw that the same manufacturer came out with a travel bottle set, I knew that I wanted it! All of their products are so well-designed and thoughtful; these bottles are made of lightweight material, and they haven't leaked yet. They also come in a super cute lightweight pouch. — Sarah Aswell.

Recent findings suggest that my husband travels for work, so he flies multiple times per week. He’s been using the Airback MAX for about a year now, and it has held up remarkably well to his strenuous schedule! But what he really loves is that it lets him skip checking a bag because it has a built-in vacuum system that sucks air out of your clothes. That means you can fit 25+ items in this one carry-on-sized bag. It also converts from a rolling trolley to a backpack in seconds, has dual TSA-approved locks, USB ports, and an expandable compression bag that doubles as a laundry bag. — Julie Sprankles.

The scariest part of any flight is wondering how long the entertainment is going to last, and this kit is built to keep toddlers 18 months and up busy from takeoff to landing without a single screen. It comes with a first-flight storybook that helps set expectations before you board, which is a small thing that makes a big difference when a little one has never been on a plane. It’s compact, screen-free, and designed by Lovevery’s play experts, so it’s one more thing I don’t have to worry about in the carry-on. — Katie Garrity.

For a bag that barely weighs a pound when unpacked and tucks away neatly into a small zippered square, you’ll be shocked by how much The Foldie actually holds: When fully expanded, it has a 40-liter packing volume. The expandable bottom adds just the right amount of extra space when needed. We love that it’s a great size to use as your carry-on or to tuck into your suitcase for bringing home souvenirs. I’ve been using this bag heavily for almost two years now, and it’s still one of my absolute favorites. Not only does it still look great, but I get asked about it all the time! — Julie Sprankles.

I fully admit I got one of these after seeing a social media video of a before-and-after. This thing really does depuff your face... and if you're like me, my face can get pretty puffy while traveling. Carrying this with me and having it after I get off the plane or after a long car ride just makes me feel better. And even besides the de-puffing benefits, it feels really good, too. — Sarah Aswell.

It has been revealed that I love that the Woda is the brainchild of two moms living in Charleston, South Carolina, who needed something hands-free that could be hosed down after days on the coast with their kids. For moms who love to pack up the car and head to the nearest beach as much as possible, you can’t get a better gift than this super-durable yet lightweight waterproof backpack. Made from a non-toxic EVA foam, it’s mold- and mildew-resistant, meaning she won’t have to worry about it getting funky after a day on the water. And it’s seriously roomy with a carrying capacity of up to 30 pounds! — Julie Sprankles.

Any traveler knows long flights cause blood flow in the legs to slow down since you’re seated for extended periods. That, in turn, can increase the risk of health issues like deep vein thrombosis. Compression socks are a simple way to help blood vessels work more efficiently on long flights, reducing the risk of swelling and blood clots. Trust us when we say that Dr. Motion compression socks are out here compressioning! And they come in so many cute patterns, which is so girly to say... but we don’t care. — Katie Garrity.

What did I do before packing cubes? I love these by JanSport because they are larger than most and fit perfectly in my suitcase side by side. The smaller "cube" is great for carrying an extra pair of undies and a spare shirt in my carry-on. They also have a see-through mesh front and a carrying handle, which make a huge difference. And never forget that JanSport items all come with an incredibly wonderful lifetime warranty. — Sarah Aswell.

Industry observers note that I’m a carry-on girlie whenever I can be, but some trips just require more space. And if I’m going to be checking a bag, I want it to fit everything without being too cumbersome. This Monos Medium Check-in is the perfect size because it’s roomy without being obnoxiously major. Plus, the limited-edition Mulberry color is a deep, glossy purple that is beyond dreamy! Add in the fact that it’s durable, has a TSA-accepted lock, and super-glidable wheels, and I genuinely get excited at the mere thought of packing for my next trip. — Julie Sprankles.

It’s a toss-up when it comes to what’s more vexing: using generic hotel bar soap to wash your face or having to buy newly introduced face wash when you get where you’re going because you can’t carry on your fave. That’s why I’m a significant fan of Olay Cleansing Melts. These portable cleansing squares are TSA-friendly since they’re water-activated, so you can toss ‘em in your purse or carry-on. — Kate Auletta.

Raise your hand if you’ve ever frantically patted down every pocket in an airport security line, convinced you lost your passport (me, it’s definitely me). So when I needed a new passport holder, I knew I wanted one with a bit of built-in peace of mind. This Spotminders Passport Holder Air works with Apple’s Find My app, meaning I can see exactly where my passport is in about two seconds. It’s ultra-slim but still has room for my license and a few other cards, plus a dedicated flap for boarding passes. Right now there’s a buy-two-get-one-free deal, which makes it a smart pick if you’re looking to upgrade the whole family before a substantial trip. — Julie Sprankles.

Industry observers note that for anyone who’s ever stood at the airport counter pulling a sweater out of an overstuffed suitcase, the BÉIS Large Check-In Roller is a game changer, thanks to its built-in weight indicator that tells you when you’re hitting 50 pounds before you ever leave the house. It has a durable hard-shell exterior, 360° wheels, a TSA lock, a hidden AirTag pocket, and 2 inches of expansion for the souvenirs you absolutely will bring home, and the glossy mint color means you’ll spot it on the carousel from across the room. It’s the one piece of luggage that makes a two-week family trip feel organized instead of chaotic! — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that for trips when I don’t have room for over-ear headphones, these Nothing Ear (3a) earbuds pack a ton of travel-ready power into a punchy, pocket-sized case. They have active noise cancellation and hi-res sound, plus the battery life is up to 41 hours so I don’t have to hunt for an outlet at the gate. They’re also great for using while on calls. I got the yellow colorway, and it just makes me happy every time I pull them out. — Julie Sprankles.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some Scary Mommy Editor favorites made the list too.
  • Countless new books come out every single year, and your TBR just gets longer and longer (and longer).
  • Sources indicate that “An extraordinary Trojan horse of a novel that will make your heart sing and make you want to talk to everybody you know about it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some Scary Mommy Editor favorites made the list too.

Countless new books come out every single year, and your TBR just gets longer and longer (and longer). If you’re struggling to figure out what to read before the end of the year, well, here’s some guidance. As they do each year, Amazon’s book editors have selected the best books of the year across all genres, including their top 20 overall. Some you’ve probably heard of and others may have slipped your notice until now, but here are their very top 10 for your consideration before year’s end.

Sources indicate that “An extraordinary Trojan horse of a novel that will make your heart sing and make you want to talk to everybody you know about it. Utterly magnetic, American Hagwon will change the way you think about family, sacrifice, and education. Min Jin Lee has written (another) once-in-a-lifetime read.” —Al Woodworth, Amazon Editor.

Devastated by a shocking betrayal, John and Helen Koh move their three children from Seoul to Southern California. New opportunity is everywhere for the children, while the elder Kohs find their education and experience in Korea does not translate to the States. As their friends, relatives, and enemies come and go, the family continues “nursing the almost all-consuming faith that education will lead the next generation to success and security.”.

“A sparkling, genre-busting gift of a novel, Emily St. John Mandel’s latest is dystopian fiction that shook me to my core. Spanning continents, timelines, and perhaps even universes, Exit Party makes for a glorious puzzle, one with pieces that fit together seamlessly.” —Annabel Gutterman, Amazon Editor.

It has been revealed that scary Mommy editor Katie Garrity called this novel “mind-bending.” Set in 2031, California has declared itself a republic apart from the U.S. The curfew in Los Angeles lifts for the first time in weeks, and citizens gravitate to a big party. What happens there will haunt Ari Waker, freshly out of prison after 18 years, for years to come.

“Robert Kolker’s enthralling medical mystery is both mesmerizing and heartbreaking — it asks big questions about chance and choice, what makes a full life, what we’re willing to run toward (or hide from), and how we care for each other. It’s a true story that will stick with you.” —Lindsay Powers, Amazon Editor.

Industry observers note that this is the heartbreaking true story of a family plagued by dementia as early as in their 40s due to a shared genetic mutation. In a family with nine siblings that all strike out as young adults, only the youngest child, Barb, is still home to see her mother become withdrawn and uncaring. Then, one by one, other members of the family begin losing jobs, destroying their marriages, and getting further and further away from their former selves. And it’s Barb who sets out to find answers — and a cure.”.

It has been revealed that “This was our pick for the best book of the year so far, and our love for this novel about two motherless friends coming of age in the Jim Crow South endures. A nuanced portrait of friendship, family, and race—Jones's sentences sing.” —Erin Kodicek, Amazon Editor.

Industry observers note that if you love Jones’ previous work, you will not be disappointed by Kin, noted Scary Mommy editor Sarah Aswell after reading the book in July. It follows Annie and Vernice, who have been best friends and neighbors since they were kids in Honeysuckle, Louisiana. Then, at 18, Vernice heads for Spelman College where she is pulled into a world of aspiration and connection, while Annie sets out into the world to find love and adventure. Where will their journeys take them, and will they come back to each other?

“Walking the line between hysterical and horrifying, this electric psychological thriller ruthlessly takes on cultural appropriation through a delicious cat-and-mouse game like no other. If you’re in a reading slump, Fruit Fly is the cure.” —Abby Abell, Amazon Editor.

Mallory Maddox is a washed-up author who hasn’t put out latest work in nearly a decade. All the buzz she worked so hard to earn is fading, and fast. So when she meets Leo, an unhoused addict trading sex for the things he needs, she finds her inspiration. How far will she go to write the perfect, career-saving story?”.

Industry observers note that “Never before have a 19th-century mapmaker, a scruffy, loyal dog, and a mysterious copse of trees been more enchanting. O’Farrell delivers a soaring and bewitching tale of family, and how the remote Irish peninsula where they live defines and shapes them, generation after generation.” —Al Woodworth, Amazon Editor.

Scary Mommy editor Sarah Aswell read Land in September and declared this story, about a family surviving Ireland’s Great Hunger who find a mysterious spring in the forest, may be O’Farrell’s best work yet.

“Illuminating and unforgettable, Patrick Radden Keefe’s latest delivers another knockout work of narrative nonfiction, this time telling the shocking story of how a young man got caught up in the dangerous and powerful world of Russian oligarchs and landed at the bottom of the Thames.” —Al Woodworth, Amazon Editor.

If you love documentaries and true crime podcasts, this book is a must-read. In the wee hours of the morning of November 29, 2019, cameras outside MI6 headquarters captured footage of a young man pacing back and forth before throwing himself into the river Thames. What follows is a deeply reported account of his parents’ quest to get answers about what happened to their son, and how on earth he ended up deciding to jump.

Sources indicate that “The many fans of Major Little Lies will love this follow-up, but you don’t need to have read that book or seen the show to enjoy Big Little Truths. I’ve been a fan of Liane Moriarty since her early books, and this is simply one of her very best. The dialogue is so clever, and the storytelling so engrossing, you won’t be able to put this book down.” —Sarah Gelman, Editorial Director.

Here’s how Scary Mommy editor Katie Garrity summed up the book after reading it in August: “Big Little Truths picks up 10 years later with Madeline, Celeste, Jane, Renata, and Bonnie, whose kindergartners are now teenagers navigating drugs, sex, and alcohol, which honestly sounds just as chaotic and stressful as the original but make it high school. When a mysterious stranger starts lurking around the school and the principal receives a severed finger in the mail, old secrets resurface and new ones threaten to unravel everything.”.

“This heart-pounding, reported memoir sucked me in from the first page; it’s a gripping account of resilience and perseverance that goes far beyond the headlines to reveal what really happened to Evan Gershkovich when he was snatched off the street and thrown into a Russian prison.” —Lindsay Powers, Amazon Editor.

Sources indicate that in March 2023, one year after Russia invaded Ukraine, journalist Evan Gershkovich met with a source roughly 900 miles east of Moscow. Out of nowhere, a group of masked agents bursts in, blindfolds him, and abducts him. They tell him he’s being charged as a spy before dumping him in Lefortovo prison. Instead of giving up, Evan kept reporting, all the way up until the prisoner swap that set him free.

“Two-time Pulitzer Prize winner Colson Whitehead delivers another searing page-turner of heists, gangsters, criminals, and families in this mesmerizing portrait of 1980s New York City.” —Al Woodworth, Amazon Editor.

If you love a good crime novel, don’t skip Cool Machine. It follows Ray Carney, his wife Elizabeth, and partner Pepper through years of heists, body guard gigs, and major transitions in Upcoming York’s history. At every turn he comes up against the most violent forces in the city, risking the safety of himself and his family for one more score.

Which of these books just moved straight to the top of your TBR?

This ‘unhinged’ advice for toddler moms is actually pretty genius

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that toddlers are a wild ride.
  • In a recent development, A recent Threads post from @jayonathequeen asked parents for their best “unhinged advice” for raising toddlers, and the replies poured in.
  • Sources indicate that many of the suggestions are surprisingly hinged.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that toddlers are a wild ride. They’re old enough to have opinions, verbal enough to pepper in words like “actually” and small enough to go fully boneless in the cereal aisle when overruled. But with the right frame of mind and a little patience, we can outsmart them.

In a recent development, A recent Threads post from @jayonathequeen asked parents for their best “unhinged advice” for raising toddlers, and the replies poured in. Some came from toddler room teachers, longtime nannies and even doctors. Most came from moms who’ve logged countless hours negotiating with toddlers and consulting their pediatricians. We’ve all earned our stripes, and sometimes there’s nothing like raw mom-to-mom advice.

Sources indicate that many of the suggestions are surprisingly hinged. And certainly no one’s judging.

Industry observers note that anyone who has turned around in a parking lot to find an empty space where a small person used to be knows this particular brand of panic. The thread’s most-liked reply, with nearly 18,000 hearts, went straight at the escape artist problem, and the moms underneath it kept the ideas coming.

Credit: @thriving_out_of_spite, @norcalcaro and @sksargeant via Threads.

One mom’s solution doubled as entertainment.

Credit: @champersstamers via Threads.

(If you try this one, stick with a foil balloon, since popped latex is a choking hazard for little kids.).

Toddler palates are a moving target. The food they inhaled one day is suddenly disgusting the next. A couple of moms found that a little creative branding goes a long way, at the table and beyond.

Credit: @analee_inreallife via Threads.

Brushing teeth, putting on shoes, surviving the checkout aisle. The daily stuff is where most battles originate, and, in turn, where moms get the most inventive. A common thread here is giving toddlers a sense of control while you cleverly steer the ship.

Credit: @parentnest.digital via Threads.

Credit: @suziespree via Threads.

And sometimes the smartest move is picking your battles.

Credit: @cryssinikki via Threads.

Industry observers note that when a meltdown hits, plenty of moms agreed the first move is regulating yourself. Toddlers take their emotional cues from us, so the calmer we stay, the faster they come back down.

Credit: @sin_standard via Threads.

From there, a little misdirection can work wonders.

Credit: @thenerdyderma via Threads.

Credit: @josephineadel via Threads.

Sources indicate that that sniff trick is a cousin of the viral “Jessica” trick, where a parent interrupts a meltdown by calmly calling for someone who isn’t there. Pediatrician Dr. Madison Szar told Motherly that “What’s that smell?” works just as well, since the surprise is what breaks the loop. Bonus points for the deep breaths.

And for the moments when you’re the one about to lose it, one mom has a suggestion that sounds unhinged until you hear her out.

Credit: @kaitlyn_e.a via Threads.

It has been revealed that then there are the white lies. One bedtime fib stood out as particularly clever.

Credit: @kellywills901 via Threads.

Having raised two kids, one in college and one in high school, I can attest that I lied to them. A lot. The car won’t start unless you’re buckled. It’s against the law to take your shoes off in the store. The toy store is closing, so we have to leave now. I promise you they are both 100% trustworthy, honest people.

When I was a new mom, just 21 and wildly out of my depth, I had a mentor with a toddler of her own. A yoga teacher who became a mom in her early 40s, she was a free spirit who didn’t mother through the lens of anyone else’s scrutiny. It was wild and refreshing.

In a recent development, she was willing to be inconvenienced so her son could explore and held firm when exploring teetered toward danger. She also leaned into the absurdity. At one point she’d somehow acquired a shopping cart, and when her son got grumpy, she’d load him in with a rug, some toys and their cat (I’m not kidding) and march around the neighborhood with the dog following behind.

According to recent reports, toddlers are ridiculous, and we all know it. Sometimes you have to meet the moment with the same.

📅 27 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1334 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

Jefferson Fisher Has The Secret to Getting Along Better With Absolutely Everyone

📅 27 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1334 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The lawyer, author, and influencer wants us to talk more and argue less.
  • In a recent development, if being a parent, a husband, a man, a human has taught me anything at all it’s that communication is everything.
  • It has been revealed that for once, our poor communication is not a product of big external forces — neither isolationist politics nor overcooked capitalism nor a failing of modern masculinity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The lawyer, author, and influencer wants us to talk more and argue less. He might just be onto something.

In a recent development, if being a parent, a husband, a man, a human has taught me anything at all it’s that communication is everything. Also, most of us suck at communication.

It has been revealed that for once, our poor communication is not a product of big external forces — neither isolationist politics nor overcooked capitalism nor a failing of modern masculinity. We can only blame ourselves because, hey, communicating is hard. Getting your point across to a group, your nuclear family, or one single person takes practice and discipline, mistakes and learning. I don’t think we ever get it entirely right.

Sources indicate that well, most of us don’t. There are some communicators in this world that are … blessed. Jefferson Fisher is one such individual. Fisher is a Texan, dad, husband, and personal injury attorney who has made a name for himself through social videos that teach us all how to communicate better.

Industry observers note that the videos offer pithy lessons like this: Instead of saying I disagree, “tweak it a little and say, I see things differently.” Why? “When you talk in terms of perspective, you find more connection.” Here’s another: “How I talk to my kids will affect how they talk to their kids.”.

Simple, pointed, and poignant. You can see why millions tune in.

Fisher’s goal is to make people talk more and argue less. It states just that on the cover of his fantastic, practical, wonderfully written book The Next Conversation — a must read for all of us who strive to get along a little better with those around us.

According to recent reports, we caught up with Fisher to talk about his new book and, naturally, anoint him as the latest Cool Dad. Here are some excerpts from our talk, including extras from the Cool Dad Questionnaire and his advice for the most important conversations you’ll ever have.

What’s one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood?

It has been revealed that probably more of a reckless abandon about what they ate. I grew up in just every Little Debbie from Cosmic Brownies to ... everything you could think of that was probably terrible for us, but we didn't know any different.

What does your partner love about you?

Recent findings suggest that I mean, this is my guess ... I would say what Sierra loves about me is my steadiness. When things don't go to strategy, I'm pretty rock steady. So when there is something unexpected or the kids go into what we call their midnight madness, when it's right there at bedtime and they're absolutely losing their minds, that's when I'm able to step in and I think I'm able to really notice when she's overwhelmed, and take over.

And what do you think they maybe find annoying about you?

I mean, there's lots. I'm trying to find a really good one like she finds the most annoying about me is sometimes I can be a little bit occasionally of like a party-pooper where the kids are just ... all going nuts and I'm like, "Can we just not yell so much in our house?" So there's that.

Sources indicate that probably the bigger thing she gets more annoyed about is my relationship with money. Its just money. So I'm the spender and so she is the saver. If it's something that's like, "Hey, but this would be fun, even though it's not something we exactly need right now, but it would be a cool memory," I think there's a lot of that.

What does fatherhood mean to you in our current world?

Fatherhood, with the caveat of doing it well to be a good father, I think, is knowing it's a discipline and not a destination. It's a daily devotion to putting your wife, your spouse, your partner, your kids before you. And it's this idea of ... are you inconveniencing them for your comfort or is it the opposite, are you willing to inconvenience yourself for their comfort?

Recent findings suggest that there are times where it's going to be uncomfortable. I don't want to be the one carrying all the bags all the time, but is it what my family needs in that moment in the airport? Yeah, that's what they need. Can I do it? Yeah.

I got to say that the carrying bags all the time is a wonderful metaphor.

Yeah. You're the one that is supposed to shoulder the heavy. So you're supposed to carry what they can't. I'm sure there's a similarity to this phrase of to be what others cannot, you must be willing to suffer what others will not, and so it's like that. To be the dad that others can't, you got to be able to do what others won't.

How do you better communicate with your partner in parenting? Do you think there's ways that you, something that don't apply, or do you follow the advice in your book and have great arguments and conversations with your spouse?

I wouldn't say there are things that don't apply. I would say what it would need to go deeper on is the theme of repair specifically. So you could have the mindset of arguments and that's something that's very helpful. Industry observers note that in repair, there is a lot of something as simple as, "Yes, I said that. Yes, I did that. The other is that unspokenness of knowing when something is wrong and that you feel like you might be approaching things from a different vantage. I like asking the phrase, "What's coming up?" "What's coming up for you?".

Industry observers note that instead of me saying, "What's wrong with you" or even, "What's up with you?" That tends to get a pretty defensive response. But if I say something as simple as what's coming up, there's a difference between [that and] saying, "How are you and how's your heart?".

Max Greenfield Is That Dad

📅 14 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a new film, the New Girl star plays a very good dad, naturally.
  • It has been revealed that the first thing you may observe about the dad in Netflix’s upcoming teen drama Don’t Say Good Luck is that his hair looks perfect.
  • Industry observers note that greenfield notes that understanding the character was easy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a new film, the New Girl star plays a very good dad, naturally.

It has been revealed that the first thing you may observe about the dad in Netflix’s upcoming teen drama Don’t Say Good Luck is that his hair looks perfect. That’s only the start of the aspirational cues coming from this character played by Max Greenfield. In this funny — and, yes, tear-jerking — family drama, Greenfield’s character juggles work, elementary-aged twins, a massive-feeling teen, and his wife’s cancer diagnosis. While he is at times off-kilter from all that life throws his way in the film, this dad does not bumble his way through it. In every scene, he finds ways to be the emotionally available parent and partner.

Industry observers note that greenfield notes that understanding the character was easy. “There’s so much of me that’s in that movie,” he tells Fatherly. “I felt so close to what we were doing.” It could be, perhaps, because his daughter, like the main character, is a high schooler; she has mutual friends to the lead actress, Sunny Sandler; and her experience — at least onstage, navigating high school life — just resonated.

We sat down to give Max Greenfield the Cool Dad questionnaire, and then talked about the movie, finding patience, and fighting parental anxiety — and why LA’s bagels are seriously underrated.

This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

In a recent development, I finished watching Don’t Say Good Luck today. I definitely did some crying.

They keep playing clips in these interviews that I’m doing for press, and they’ll play it before the interview, and I’m constantly like, “I need a minute.”.

In a recent development, it’s intense. It’s a wonderful film. I’m wondering how close of a dad are you to who you play on screen in Don’t Say Good Luck. Are you that dad?

I mean, there’s so much of me that’s in that movie. I felt so close to what we were doing. It was really the reason I wanted to do it. My daughter, I think, is a year younger than Sunny [Sandler, the lead], and I was really aware that this was going to be a movie that Sunny was starring in. And from everything that I had heard, I had never done a Sandler movie before, but his sets are famously the best. And so I really wanted to just make sure that she had a comparable experience on this with somebody else. I felt like I knew how to do that.

My daughter and her have mutual friends, I know where she goes to school… just a lot of the stuff I just was like, “I know this world well.” And so talking to somebody like Sunny is not an matter for me. And trying to be light and supportive in this environment, it was something I felt like I was capable of doing. I didn’t know if I was going to be very good in the movie as an actor, but I was like, “I think I know how to be the dad.” And then there’s the two young boys in the movie, the twins, and they were so funny because they were just never acting. They just were running around.

In a recent development, they’re a little bit younger than my son, but I just coached my son’s basketball team, and wrangling all those kids and getting them going, getting them involved, it was very good prep work for dealing with these two boys. And it made the scenes and made the movie so much fun.

It has been revealed that yeah. Everything was just like, “Oh, this is what my real life is.” And being there with Sunny, I understood that relationship. Being there with the boys, I was like, “I get this relationship.”.

There was a more dramatically real scene later in the movie … I personally had a similar experience to the lead character. My mom had cancer when I was a sophomore in high school, and all I could think about was how I wanted you — your character — to be my dad for that time. For example, that scene when you were sitting in the car and Sunny asked, “Are you okay?” And you asked, “Are you okay?” And both of you remarked, “No.” It was just… right.

That was a really cool scene. Julia Hart, who had directed the movie and wrote the movie along with Laura Hankin and Jordan Horowitz … [had] a lot of conversations about that scene, and they were so generous in my input. It really felt like that scene was going to be the scene for this relationship. And as we started to see how the movie was playing out and what was happening before then, we had sent a bunch of drafts of that scene back and forth to one another, and we all collectively landed in that spot because it really needed to set up everything that comes after that, but it needed to honor everything that was built up before it, and it needed to feel real.

It has been revealed that I didn’t want there to be an answer or a fix to what was happening, but I wanted them to feel it, both characters. When we shot that scene, it was nuts. It was really heavy, man.

Recent findings suggest that in this movie, you run a bagel shop. So what’s your order?

Industry observers note that oh, wow. Great question. I’ve probably gotten older and more healthy than I need to be, more LA than I need to be. I’ll give you two. One’s an everything bagel [with] just cream cheese, onion, tomato, lox.

That can’t ever miss, it’s the best. The other one is … either a light cream cheese spread [or] the right type of hummus and then just veggies. But fresh, good veggies that are with the right type of dressing on it and salt and pepper. There’s a place in LA that has been hyped and hyped and I finally went there, I don’t know, a month or two ago. It’s called Courage Bagels. And the line is a mile long. And I was like, “I’m not waiting in line.” And then my daughter and I were like, “Let’s go wait in line.” So we went over there and they had one, I think it’s called the Garden or something. I don’t know. Holy sh*t. It was unbelievable.

Industry observers note that one of the significant themes of the movie I wanted to get your take on is disclosure to children. That is, what you tell a kid, what you don’t tell a kid, when you’re protecting them from the truth, and when that backfires. I was just wondering if you had thoughts on how you strike that personally.

It’s a really good question. I actually feel like I’ve done a good job with this, personally. There are certain things that I want them to discover on their own, and hopefully my job is to have created a space where they feel comfortable to then bring those things up to me. And then depending on how the question’s asked or how much they want to know, you ease them into certain topics of discussion and what you choose to discover based on what they’re asking. And you let that conversation be ongoing. And so I’ve had some real good success in some areas where those conversations have opened up and become more in-depth over time. And as a result, I see that my kids are way more comfortable with information that I was worried might be confusing or scary. And because they’ve sort of been able to take it in at their pace.

How has your outlook changed now that you’re past the baby and elementary parenting and you have a 16- and 11-year-old?

Industry observers note that I’m making a lot more mistakes. That thing we talked about, responsibility versus what to let go, that line is thinner and thinner every day. And there’s so many times where, what are the things that I feel like I need to control to make me feel safer in this situation that is so scary? And being a fear-based parent is not a good zone to operate from.

And so it’s like my daughter’s now driving and she gets her driver’s license and it’s just like, my wife and I are both like, “Well, so the next day, is she just driving to volleyball practice? Is that how that works?” And if you strip all the fear away from it, you’re like, “Yeah, she practiced and worked up to it and has now passed the test and she’s allowed to legally drive. So yes, why wouldn’t she be able to?” There’s a period of time when they’re small where you’re like, “Yeah, this is just going to keep getting better.” And then it shifts in the most terrifying way and you’re like, “Oh, this is all so much worse.”.

When we were [learning to drive], I would sit in the car with her, we would drive, and I would go, “Oh, you know what? All the anxiety and fear I have about the future and life and work and all the nonsense, that’s not real.” When I’m sitting in a car with my daughter and she’s driving, this is real fear. This is what real fear feels like. It’s like, this is the shark in the water kind of fear. And it’s heavy and it’s tangible. And you almost hold it and you go, “This is what real fear feels like, and this is appropriate for the situation.” So outside of that, when I do feel any sort of anxiety about the future or whatever it is, I go, “Oh, this is not real.” And now I know the difference. So at least I have that.

Breaking: How To Give Medicine To A Child Who Refuses: Tips For Sensitive Kids

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1442 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A pediatrician and a nurse practitioner share how to get medicine, saline, and bandages past kids who’d rather do anything else, plus how to handle the guilt afterward.
  • According to recent reports, has your child ever run around the house to avoid having their scraped-up knee cleaned and bandaged?
  • All kids are miserable when they are sick, but for children who are neurodivergent, have disabilities, and/or sensory sensitivities, symptoms can feel more intense and be more challenging to manage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A pediatrician and a nurse practitioner share how to get medicine, saline, and bandages past kids who’d rather do anything else, plus how to handle the guilt afterward.

According to recent reports, has your child ever run around the house to avoid having their scraped-up knee cleaned and bandaged? Does a dose of antibiotics require two adults, one to immobilize and one to administer the medication? And potentially a change of clothing for you and/or your child afterwards? If so, you might have a sensitive sick kid.

All kids are miserable when they are sick, but for children who are neurodivergent, have disabilities, and/or sensory sensitivities, symptoms can feel more intense and be more challenging to manage. And it always seems that the kids who struggle the most are the ones who will inevitably catch every bug. Unfortunately, my family is a regular fixture at our pediatrician’s office and our local CVS pharmacy as a result.

Sources indicate that medication administration is not easy for a lot of parents. And during illnesses such as the flu, strep throat, or ear infections, a whole host of medications may be recommended for pain, fever reduction, or coughs. While some of these medications are available in “kid-friendly” flavors, it doesn’t mean that your sensitive kiddo is going to agree with that assessment. Board-certified pediatrician Dr. Lauren Hughes recommends that parents choose their battles, because many medications, while helpful in ideal circumstances, aren’t critical for recovery.

Recent findings suggest that “There is no real good data for vapor rubs or OTC cough meds in kids under 6 years. Honestly, my favorite cough medicine [for] children is just a spoonful of honey,” says Hughes. “When it comes to things like ibuprofen and acetaminophen, these are helpful for controlling pain and discomfort, which can often help the child feel better so they will continue drinking and staying hydrated. However, a fever itself is not harmful in children over 60 days with normal immune systems.”.

Lindsay McHugh, DNP, a board-certified psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner and co-founder of Resting Roo, recommends that parents of children who have difficulty taking medications experiment with other ways to ease symptoms. “You [can] try heating packs to alleviate pain or ice packs, or if they have a stuffy, you could warm that up in the microwave, and they could hold it on a certain spot,” McHugh claims, “[For fever] a warm bath or a lukewarm or even a cool bath, whatever feels right to your child at the time… to make them as comfortable as possible.”.

It has been revealed that both McHugh and Hughes say taking the full course of antibiotics if prescribed needs to be parents’ priority. “If we don’t take [all] the antibiotics, then they could potentially build a resistance,” notes McHugh. “If they build a resistance, then we have even sicker kids for even longer.”.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, antibiotics — which can taste disgusting and/or have gritty textures — can be the biggest medication battle. Hughes has the following recommendations:.

An absolute game changer in our family has been my daughter learning to swallow pills. Now I wish we had tried it much sooner. McHugh says that while some 3-year-olds might be ready, parents usually can start trying with their children at age 4 or 5. “[You can start] practicing with certain foods that are somewhat pill-shaped, not too big, something soft… like a pea,” says McHugh, “[And say], ‘Let’s practice trying to not chew your pea. Let’s practice trying to swallow it.’ Practice outside of being sick. So then when they are sick, then it’s not so foreign.”.

Once my daughter got the hang of it, it changed everything: When she needed antibiotics a couple months later, the pediatrician was able to prescribe pills she could swallow.

Our entire family has a history of sensitive skin, allergies, and skin ailments like eczema. These seem to frequently coexist in individuals with other sensory sensitivities. Both my daughter and I, for example, can react to the adhesive in some Band-Aids. Now we use Band-Aids for Sensitive Skin for her or, alternatively, sensitive skin tape and non-stick gauze for protecting and healing cuts and injuries.

Recent findings suggest that while it’s ideal to only use products that you know your child likes and doesn’t react to, sometimes you need to make a change or try something fresh for a symptom or illness you haven’t encountered before. For items with topical application, McHugh recommends checking out Environmental Working Group’s Skin Deep database to research products that may include ingredients you know your child is allergic or sensitive to or might cause a reaction.

McHugh recommends trying out new topical items on an area of the body where your child is the least sensitive (which will be different for every child), while they are healthy. “Pick a 1x1 or a 2x2 inch square, and try the product, a little bit at a time. I would…see how they [and] how their skin responds,” claims McHugh, “So maybe on day two or three we do this whole leg [and] see if that’s not too overwhelming from skin sensitivity as well as the smell or feel.”.

Since my daughter and I are both sensitive to smells, I also have her smell-test products in the store aisle before we buy.

Since I have a kiddo who is sensitive to touch and texture even when she is feeling 100%, standard oral thermometers have pretty much been a no-go since she was an infant, and temporal thermometers can be tricky on a sweaty kid who doesn’t like to be touched. A no-touch forehead thermometer gets a quick read without any contact, and one with a silent mode lets you take overnight temps without waking them.

Illness can be especially tricky for younger children who can’t (or won’t) blow their noses. But Hughes says it is especially critical for infants who are under six months who are still exclusively breast- or bottle-fed: When they’re congested, they can’t breathe while feeding and are likely to become dehydrated.

Industry observers note that for using inhalers, nasal aspirators, and nasal saline, Hughes recommends the following hold: “The adult sits down with their legs spread in a V. They put the child’s head up between their legs and then place the child’s arms under their thighs. The parent then crosses their shins/ankles over the child’s legs to hold them in place. This allows the parent to have both hands free while the child is immobilized without harming them.”.

Here are some other tips for treatment of congestion, drainage, and coughs:.

Sources indicate that illnesses and injuries can be exhausting for sensitive kids and their parents. And it can be easy to start feeling guilty for having to force your child to take medicine or do some other treatment that was uncomfortable, even if it was best for them and helped them feel better in the long term. This can be especially challenging if you are trying to teach your children about bodily autonomy and boundaries.

McHugh recommends that parents try to be clear before these moments about what you are going to have to do, that you are taking care of them, they are safe, and that you know that it may be uncomfortable, painful, or taste yucky.

Recent findings suggest that “[After] I would offer empathy [and] validate their experience,” says McHugh, “And then I would say, ‘I know in the past we've talked about body autonomy, body safety. And it feels like Mommy and Daddy broke that. I’m sorry that we did that… However, we have to take care of you, and your safety is our number one priority.’”.

When our kids are sick or have an injury, it’s a high-stress time. You’re worried about your child, but you’re also worried about doing the right thing and taking care of them the right way. And sometimes you need to do what you need to do, whether it is accepting help from those around you, asking for a break, or yes, bribing your child to cooperate with some part of their care.

Recent findings suggest that “When your child isn’t feeling good, you’re already on edge. It’s most appropriate to treat [them] so that they don’t get sicker, and we want to take care of our babies and do everything we can. And if it takes a couple extra popsicles…that’s perfectly okay,” reflects McHugh, “Don’t forget to take care of yourself; it’s the last thing on the list. But [sometimes] you just need a little break to go to the bathroom and cry, because it was awful.”.

#90468. Nick Viall Opens Up About Fatherhood
