📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

Nick Viall Opens Up About Fatherhood

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2093 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nick Viall first appeared on “The Bachelorette” 12 years ago and ever since, he’s had one serious reality TV run.
  • What viewers might not know is that this Wisconsinite, the second oldest of 11 siblings, has a two-year-old and, since July, twin infants.
  • According to recent reports, how's being a twin dad going?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nick Viall on love, life, and being a twin dad.

Nick Viall first appeared on “The Bachelorette” 12 years ago and ever since, he’s had one serious reality TV run. From “Bachelor in Paradise” to “Dancing With the Stars,” “The Masked Singer” to “Age of Attraction,” which he presently co-hosts with his wife, Natalie Joy Viall , his handsome mug is everywhere. He also notably doles out relationship advice, also alongside his wife, on the The Viall Files, one of the most popular relationship podcast on Apple that airs three to four times a week.

What viewers might not know is that this Wisconsinite, the second oldest of 11 siblings, has a two-year-old and, since July, twin infants. So how’s twin dad life? “When you tell people you're expecting ... people are more prone to just kind of, I call doomsday kind of advice,” he tells Fatherly. “And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing.” We caught up to give Nick the Cool Dad questionnaire and it seems he didn’t want it to end. “It's fun to talk about fatherhood,” he states. Which is good, because he’s got a lot of fathering on his hands right now.

According to recent reports, how's being a twin dad going? I have had friends who were twin parents, and it's so … much.

According to recent reports, overall, it's great. I mean, I think every stage is different. With newborns — it sounds like you're a father as well, so as you know — they're just little potatoes at first. And for the most part, other than the regular feedings and having to wake up multiple times in the middle of the night, which can get tiring, it's not too bad. But obviously those moments … pockets of overwhelmingness of like, "Oh, no." One cries, and then you calm one down, and then another one cries.

For the most part, I was joking with Natalie, my wife, about it honestly, because you get so nervous about twins. A lot of times when you tell people you're expecting ... People are more prone to just kind of give what I call doomsday advice where it's like, "Oh, get ready for hell," or something like that. And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing For the most part, it just feels like you got a BOGO, like a buy one, get one free. And it's like, great. Obviously, my wife during the pregnancy, different experience. Obviously, I think it's a lot more on mothers to carry two than one.

But it's been really exciting to just be like, "Oh, we already have three kids, and it only took two pregnancies." So easy for me to say, obviously, but it's been really fun.

Industry observers note that well, congratulations. The first question I have is just wondering what kind of dad are you?

I'm a pretty involved dad and pretty hands-on. Natalie and I, ever since we've been together, we just share the responsibilities of our household. And that was true even before we became parents. I was lucky enough to have the parents I had. And I think that the biggest takeaway I had from my childhood is just how my parents worked as a team.

In a recent development, I have 10 brothers and sisters. And my parents were very lower middle class, very blue collar. My mom stayed home and worked. I mean, my mom stayed home and raised the kids, my dad worked, but that wasn't based on some kind of a decision they made. It was more like that was the situation they had.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of the day-to-day, they shared their responsibility. My mom did a lot of the traditional day-to-day keeping up the house, but my dad would often make dinner. My mom sometimes would mow the lawn. It was just more like all hands on deck type of thing, and you just do things as a team. And that's just something Natalie and I implemented into our relationship early on. And then, obviously, when River showed up, it continued. And then Natalie started working with me on the show.

According to recent reports, and so really we're just very involved. And so any little thing I can do to help Natalie or just be an involved parent, we're doing things together every step of the way.

So I'm just hyper-involved. There's no her thing, my thing. We conquer and divide, and certainly, we joke where I'm allergic to laundry, she's allergic to dishes. I don't mind doing dishes. She doesn't mind doing laundry. So there's definitely things that we have our preferences, but for the most part, we just share everything.

Nick Viall and Natalie Joy Viall have many joint ventures including, namely, the uber-successful Viall Files relationship advice podcast.

What's one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood or will have?

It has been revealed that well, I feel very fortunate to say that I was lucky enough to try to be able to give the best part of my childhood to my children because I was lucky enough to buy back my grandfather's lake house a couple years ago. And that was a place that in my childhood was like my Nirvana. It was my special place.

Sadly, when my grandfather passed away when I was in the fourth grade, they sold that property, and it was like this devastating moment of my life. It was like some real childhood trauma.

And it was a place that, quite frankly, I had recurring dreams all the way into adulthood. And again, I was lucky enough to buy it back and just really excited that it will be a place that I'll hopefully be able to give to my children, and a place that they'll be able to grow up and we'll have, obviously, a lot of hopefully monumental family events there. So that's definitely something I want them to have.

Sources indicate that but thinking in the vein of how times might be different, I think the world's changing so fast. I have such fond memories of going to the movies as a child, going to Blockbuster and picking on a movie and things like that. And some of those moments I hope we'll still be able to do. Or just maybe I hope there's a renaissance of people wanting to get outside, touch grass type of thing. And I hope that's something our children will be able to enjoy.

And certainly, in the lake houses up in the middle of nowhere in Wisconsin will be a great tool to help our kids want to be outside and play in nature and just make-believe. Most of my childhood was a lot of just make believe with my friends outside. And we would ride our bikes all over the place.

In a recent development, it's weird. I'm sure you're probably familiar with that book, The Anxious Generation by Jonathan … he talked about the freedoms that kids used to have back in the day and parents like 5, 10 years ago got a little... it's like you get nervous about the world, but you took for granted, again, the dangers of the phone. And so I'm really hoping my kids get to embrace the world and get outside and play make believe with their friends and things like that. So that's a big focus for us and certainly, hopefully, something that I hope they do get to enjoy because those are always fond memories that I have as a child.

That's a great perspective. I mean, I do agree that right now is a good time to have kids because everyone is much more aware of the difficulties parents are facing . You'll see all the support in elementary school. It's really talked about a lot.

And on to the next question: What does your wife love about you?

Well, I think probably just the fact that, I hope, that I like to think I'm her rock. There's so much burden and pressure on moms postpartum. I like to think that my job is just to be a cheerleader. When I get a sense that she's stressed out or feeling overwhelmed, I'm quick to try to give her a break, tell her to go lie down if that's what she wants to do. I'm always there and always available.

Recent findings suggest that and I hope that's one thing that she loves most about me, but I just try to be as supportive as possible just to remind her and just be a cheerleader. Just always remind her that she's doing a great job because, again, there's just so much pressure that moms put on themselves.

The other side of that coin, what does she maybe find annoying about you?

In a recent development, oh, my God, the list is so long. Well, I don't know how to close a cupboard. I don't put things away. I leave a trail of destruction wherever I go. I'm messier than our two-year-old. So there is that.

Sources indicate that I've recently got back into some video game playing, which definitely gives her the ick, but she is kind enough to let me decompress with a game here or there. So I think she'd prefer it not to exist, but … everything in moderation. Again, the trick for any dad out there who enjoys a video game or two is to never let it get in the way of being helpful. So that's the trick to get it in when you can, but never let it come in the way of, obviously, being a partner and being a father.

What does fatherhood mean to you in the current world?

Recent findings suggest that I mean, it means everything to me. I've had this conversation with a lot of peers that I have, and I have a lot of women friends in the space I work in, and so talked to some upcoming young mothers, young professionals who, obviously, their careers are and still are really key to them.

Once you have a child, I describe it as the easiest North Star. I've been fortunate enough in my life to accomplish a lot of cool things and it's nice to have individual accomplishments and accolades and awards, but they're not always as fulfilling as you think they might be when they happen. Fatherhood, parenthood is just... you always know why you're doing something. You always know what the purpose is. And so even the late nights, it's a drag to get up at 2:00 in the morning, but you know why you're doing it, and you always get a sense of purpose and accomplishment. And it's just the best motivator. No matter what's going on in work or in our personal life, it really calms you down.

I'm a fairly anxious, high-stress guy. It's easy for me to get worried about work and all the things that are going on in this world. And then I have the benefit of coming home, and especially with River now when she greets me. I'm constantly on my phone with work, and I'm never not working in a sense, but when I walk into the house, Natalie's incorporated this kind of best practice of making sure I'm off my phone and I'm very present to greet River. Even if it's for a few minutes, even if I still have some work left to do, I never walk in on the phone and I'm not giving her my undivided attention. And it's something like Natalie incorporated, which I really appreciate that she did, and I think it's just a really great best practice that we do.

Thank you so much for all the thoughtful answers.

Industry observers note that I appreciate it, man. It's fun to talk about fatherhood.

According to recent reports, it's something I really enjoy. And it's weird because in my... I don't know if you've noticed this. I mean, it's weird how parenting has become, like everything else these days, almost like a polarizing topic. No parent is indifferent about parenting, and obviously, every parent comes with passion, but it's weirdly become a topic that I'd want to talk about more, but sometimes it's like you want to be careful because you don't want to force your thoughts and feelings onto others.

The real must-haves, how to prevent diaper rash from day one, and where your budget actually matters.

They don’t need a 12-step skincare routine, and you don’t have to buy a wipe warmer to be a good parent.

According to recent reports, pediatric guidance necessitates a much shorter list than your feed does. Here’s what you actually need to focus on.

You’ll be changing a lot of diapers every day, so one of the most vital things you can do is establish a good diapering routine. This is what you need within arm’s reach:.

Sources indicate that it all comes down to what’s in the wipe and how reactive your baby’s skin is. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises avoiding fragrances, dyes, and parabens on infant skin, so that's a good place to start.

The bottom line: For most newborns, a fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipe is just fine. Don't worry about water wipes unless your baby's skin reacts to everything.

It has been revealed that most diaper rash is the byproduct of moisture and friction, so the best way to prevent it is to establish a good changing routine. Here’s what the AAP advises:.

Call your pediatrician if the rash:.

Babies are not cheap! You'll be blowing through roughly 240 to 360 diapers a month. Here are some ways you can save:.

Prioritize fit and leak protection.

According to recent reports, make your diaper budget work for you. Fewer leaks and blowouts mean fewer outfit changes (and fewer middle-of-the-night sheet swaps). So, the convenience alone will pay for itself. You don’t even have to trade up to a premium line to get it: Mainstream Pampers lines like Swaddlers and Baby Dry cover the pediatric-aligned basics. Weigh a subscription vs. buying separately.

Here are five picks, drilled down by category:.

What are the best newborn care essentials to buy before the baby arrives?

Sources indicate that stick to the basics: a safe sleep surface, an infant car seat, diapering supplies (diapers, wipes, barrier cream, and a changing surface), a few onesies, and whatever your feeding plan requires. Everything else can wait.

Should I get sensitive-skin wipes or water wipes for newborn diaper changes?

Recent findings suggest that fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipes meet pediatric guidance for everyday newborn use. Water wipes are an extra-cautious option for babies who have eczema-prone or very reactive skin.

What newborn essentials are best for preventing diaper rash from day one?

Industry observers note that two non-negotiables: Change diapers frequently and use a zinc-oxide or petrolatum-based barrier cream. A well-fitting, absorbent diaper helps too.

Should I prioritize premium diapers or sensitive wipes in my newborn essentials budget?

Prioritize diaper fit and leak protection first, since that’s what keeps moisture off skin (and blowouts off clothes). Then save on wipes: A fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipe covers most babies without specialty pricing.

Is a diaper subscription bundle or buying essentials separately a better value for newborns?

In a recent development, this is really a convenience-vs-flexibility call. Diaper subscription bundles offer discounts the more you buy and can spare you store runs. Buying separately lets you switch sizes as your baby grows — which happens fast in the newborn stage!

What are the best newborn care essentials to buy in 2026?

The same ones as always. The core list (sleep surface, car seat, diapering, clothes, and feeding) hasn’t changed in 2026; there are just more options. You still need a snug/leakproof diaper, fragrance-free wipes, a zinc-oxide barrier cream, and a portable changing pad.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.

In a recent development, it’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee. Or that on his first job overseeing the dog kennel in an amusement park (apparently a thing), he let the dog out (“it was a whole thing … and that was kind of the end of the dog kennel”). Or even the basic fact that at the height of his career he decided to move back to Tennessee so that his teen daughter might have a more normal life. Bargatze’s life, like his comedic work, reads like a folksy tall tale. It draws you in with the details and lulls you with its sense of warmhearted authenticity — then lands a punchline.

Industry observers note that but authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years. He recently brought some of his experience to Ford’s Accelerate conference, where he is a spokesperson for what they’re calling the “essential economy” — of skilled technicians and tradespersons, a group that, according to economists, is in short supply and needs to grow. Bargatze is an interesting choice for this forum, a comedian with a high school degree and no formal trade skills besides those he learned onstage. He went to community college for a year and worked a variety of jobs, from waiting at Applebee’s to reading water meters. But he gets the value and opportunity in trade school. “I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools. I did not go to college ... They’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, crucial for just the future.”.

Nate Bargatze poses with students at the Ford Accelerate conference, which he mc-ed.

He also is thinking about this because his 14-year-old is not too far from entering the workforce. “Right now it’s like, yeah, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it. But then, as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room, so you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to [instill that urgency] as a parent. And if you don’t, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you.” Which all boils down to a most authentic parenting philosophy: “Be a good example, basically.”.

Tell me about what you’re doing right now at this Ford Accelerate event.

Industry observers note that what Ford is doing with this event that we’re at right now, where they’re showing kids going into trade schools ... letting kids know that this is kind of the future, that they’re going to have jobs. And it’s like we don’t know where jobs are going with AI and all this stuff, but the trade schools… We need that. I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools.

It has been revealed that I worked the water meters. I did not go to college. They’re going to get more college than I did. But they’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future. I think they’re putting themselves in such a great position, probably better than they realize now, but they’re going to, I think, look back and just be like, “Man, that was such a good call.”.

I’m wondering, since we’re talking about work, what’s the most crucial thing you’ve learned about work in your life?

According to recent reports, I always go back to when I waited tables at one point and our manager there always talked about a sense of urgency. And that’s always stuck with me for some reason. It was just going to a table and just have a sense of urgency. It goes a long way when you get to that table and they really feel like they’re being taken care of. I think I’ve just kept that even as I’ve gone forward. If you respond to emails or my team is talking to you, I don’t want to be like, “I’ll get to them next week.” You kind of want to just be like, “No, let’s get to them and let’s make sure that we stay on top of it.”.

Nate Bargatze plays an off-the-rails George Washington when he hosted SNL in 2024.

Speaking of people who don’t have it, how do you instill that sense of urgency in your kid without them fighting back?

You say stuff as a parent, you don’t know what’s sticking and what’s not sticking. You keep talking about it, and the older she gets — she’s 14 now — the more she’s going to see examples of it. Right now, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it, but then as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room. So you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to do it as a parent. And if you don’t do it, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you. And so, be a good example, basically.

Then what’s one thing you wish your kids had today that you had during your childhood?

It has been revealed that I think not the internet, maybe. That would be something, even though it’s great and the connection and it’s all this stuff, you just wish they would’ve had a little more... I think innocence lasted longer when we grew up because you just weren’t pounded with information all day long.

What’s your wife love about you?

Recent findings suggest that I hope me for being me. We’ve been together before any of this started. We met at Applebee’s. Our 20th wedding anniversary is Oct. 13. I think it’s taking time to get used to it, but we’re along this ride together and just the surprises. We don’t know where everything’s going to end up or what’s going to happen. I think that she sees that I work hard at stuff and has been behind the scenes and loved me before any of this and loves me now. So it’s just to have the support from her, I wouldn’t be here without her. And she very much kept me grounded in a world when you come up in comedy that you could not be... It’s easy to not be grounded.

On the flip side, what do they maybe find annoying about you?

It has been revealed that she doesn’t like eating near me because she thinks I’d chew loud. I don’t think I’m too loud. I think it’s very normal. But she gets very uncomfortable if she’s like... I mean, if she’s on the couch and I’m at the table right behind the couch, she cannot stand it. So I eat outside now — and I only do soups.

What kind of dad are you? How would you describe yourself as a dad?

In a recent development, I like to be... You find moments to talk to your kid. As they get older, they have friends. She’s young and all that, so they want to run with their friends. A massive part is finding the moments of when they can get very talkative, and so you can find these little pockets and really try to home in on those.

In a recent development, she knows I’m a fun time. She can take me for a ride, where her mom can put her foot down a little bit more. She knows where to go. She thinks very much like me, and she can work you if she wants something, and she works me quite a bit.

Coming back to the work thing, what was your first job?

Industry observers note that my first job, I worked at Opryland Theme Park in Nashville. I was 15, and so I was a sweeper. I walked around and just swept up the park. And I also did the dog kennel. After the sweeper, I got promoted to dog kennel.

Nate Bargatze with his wife, Laura Bargatze.

Well, because people would bring their pets because they’re on vacation and they’d travel with their pets.

So you can’t bring them to the park. And so people would bring their dogs in or whatever, their cats. I think we had a chicken. People travel with some weird animals. But one dog got out, and so it was a whole thing. And that was kind of the end of the dog kennel. I think I went back to sweeping after that. But he got out, and so we had to call the... again, pre-internet, so you got to announce to the park, “Whose German shepherd got out in the parking lot?” And then they got to go search for this dog and it was under a parked car. And yeah, I still talk to that family today.

Industry observers note that I’m sure you don’t. They don’t want to talk to you.

Industry observers note that no. But I bet they still remember it. We both still remember that.

AJ McLean on his solo “The Better Man” Tour.

What's the best film to watch with kids?

What's one thing you wish your kids had today that you had growing up, especially as a kid from the ’80s?

There was no Bose surround sound, there was none of that.".

It has been revealed that and then my youngest — last year as a birthday present from one of her friends — got a Discman. And she of course put the CD in upside down, I had to show her the right way. That was painful. But she really loves her freaking Discman. She loves it. And I love that they're starting to come back where you actually have to buy the CD. What's music have you successfully introduced your kids to?

Fatherhood, to me, means protection. It means compassion, understanding. Sources indicate that they're not shy by any means. They will talk to everybody and talk their ear off, and I have no idea where they get that from. But yeah, I try to just really set an example, especially as a father and as a man, I want my daughters to look at me and then be able to say when the time comes that they want to date boys, this is what a boy should be. And I grew up single-parent household, so I grew up to very much so respect women to the utmost, and put them up on a pedestal, which it's kind of a give and take, but to really know that none of us would be here without a woman, let's just say that.

I mean, I'm a sneakerhead. I have a problem. And I've gotten my girls into it now, which my wife is so thrilled about.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The coziness of the holidays gets me all sentimental.
  • I know this now that I am grown and trying to figure out if I’m a good cook myself.
  • Sources indicate that her baking though, now that was good.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The coziness of the holidays gets me all sentimental.

My Nana was not a good cook. Not really. Her food was always basic. Good, but basic. I know this now that I am grown and trying to figure out if I’m a good cook myself. She was Irish and had about 12 things she knew how to cook and they were basically all holiday menu-specific. She could do up a roast turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, gravy. A bag of coleslaw with a bottle of creamy dressing tossed in. She bought those little grocery store dinner rolls and popped them in the oven to warm as my Grandpa carved the turkey, his only chance to shine in the winter season as the barbeque was no longer an option.

Sources indicate that her baking though, now that was good. A bit better than good by ‘80s standards since the Great British Baking Show didn’t exist. She made excellent sticky buns and little donuts she shook in paper bags of cinnamon and sugar while they were piping hot. She baked birthday cakes for all of the grandchildren, chocolate and peanut butter, or strawberry cream, or white cake with jam in the middle.

Recent findings suggest that most of all, she baked raisin bread. Loaf after loaf of raisin bread for everyone she knew. We’ve never found the recipe in the two decades that she has been gone, and it is the thing her whole family misses the most. The dark, molasses smell of it. A nod to her Nova Scotian heritage. Sturdy enough to toast if you cut your morning slab extra thick. Sturdy enough for a great substantial smear of peanut butter too. A singular flavor I will miss forever.

Recent findings suggest that her raisin bread and cinnamon buns and chocolate cakes were not the things that drew us all to her kitchen. Her turkey wasn’t even really moist enough to have us all clamoring for late night sandwiches, and yet there we stood. Every year. Daughters and sons, grandchildren, friends. Some of us in pajamas, others in track pants to accommodate our food babies. My quiet Grandpa hovering around the periphery, hoping someone would make him a plate of food. We came for the sandwich but mostly we came for her. My Nana. A short, bossy, contrary matriarch who made messes, made toast with marmalade on cold mornings, made cup after cup of tea left too long on the stove.

She made me want to be just like her. To call my loves back to my own kitchen. To make people feel welcome and loved and relaxed and just seen, all the time she was seeing us out of the corner of her eye. “What’s wrong?” she’d ask me as she was kneading cinnamon-scented dough for her raisin bread, all casual and relaxed as a viper ready to strike. She knew, she always knew, we came to her kitchen to pray at her feet. To talk out a breakup or a fresh love or a money problem over plates of eggs fried too hard, bread toasted too long. Almost always with a toddler sitting at her feet, a baby on her hip. A smile on her face.

Her technique in the kitchen was really more of a siren song. She chose her smells wisely, I think. She favoured cinnamon over chocolate. Rosemary over garlic. Warm hug smells. Luring us in for a gossip, her favorite appetizer for any meal. Did you hear? Guess who’s dating? You didn’t hear this from me… A buffet of talking and food, of mess and chaos.

According to recent reports, it has been 20 years since she died. I am as old as she was when I was a little girl, our golden hour together. And yet, she looms as large now in my holiday kitchen as she did when I was a girl.

Recent findings suggest that it is her voice I hear when I call out to my own sons, “Who’s hungry?” and make us all a significant pot of chili to eat while we watch The Lord of the Rings for the hundredth time in the dark quiet of our living room. Or a great stack of buttermilk pancakes to be eaten with overly crisp bacon and real maple syrup, all of us sleepy at our table.

It was even her voice I heard in my oldest son when he told me he would like to take over Christmas morning breakfast. I sat in the kitchen, a cup of tea at my elbow, as he and his brothers made eggs benedict for all of us. One making artful pour over coffee, another seasoning hashbrowns, still another carefully poaching eggs and adding lemon to his homemade bechamel.

The food has improved, but the heart of it stays the same. We come back to this kitchen that is not her kitchen but also is her kitchen.

According to recent reports, jen McGuire is a contributing writer for Romper and Scary Mommy. She lives in Canada with four boys and teaches life writing workshops where someone cries in every class. When she is not traveling as often as possible, she’s trying to organize pie parties and outdoor karaoke with her neighbors. She will sing Cher’s “If I Could Turn Back Time” at least once, but she’s open to requests.

How to thank school support staff this American Education Week (Hint: It’s not a mug)

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (585 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that my son’s favorite person in elementary school was the nurse.
  • That nurse lovingly cared for kids who needed far more support than my son did.
  • People like her have a name in education circles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that my son’s favorite person in elementary school was the nurse. She was warm and welcoming, always quick with a comforting hug. More importantly, she had the best Band-Aids in the building, and she wasn’t stingy about giving them out. A scraped knee got one. So did a paper cut, and even some invisible injuries, too. She knew when a kid headed to see her, it wasn’t necessarily about needing that Band-Aid.

That nurse lovingly cared for kids who needed far more support than my son did. There were kids who came to her office with a belly ache that wasn’t a stomach bug, but because they hadn’t had breakfast, and possibly dinner either. There were kids who could barely stay awake in class because they’d spent the night in a car instead of a bed. She met those kids with the same warmth she gave my Band-Aid collector, and I’m certain she kept a stash of snacks in her desk for those visits in particular.

People like her have a name in education circles. They’re education support professionals, or ESPs, and they include school nurses, cafeteria workers, bus drivers, security staff, paraeducators, technical personnel, custodians, skilled trade workers, and front office staff. Ask kids about their favorite grown-up at school, and there’s a decent chance the answer is one of them.

The people our kids adore are often the people schools pay the least. Nearly 32% of full-time ESPs earn less than $25,000 a year, according to the National Education Association, and on average, they’re paid below a living wage in all 50 states.

That’s not a livable wage in most areas. “Our wages are so low, we are forced to have two or three jobs,” paraeducator Yahaira Rodriguez told NEA Today. The nurse who stays late with a hungry kid may be heading to a second job after school, eating dinner in the car on the way. That’s a long day for someone whose job is to take care of everyone else’s kids. It also makes it hard to stay in the job. Before the 2024–25 school year, 69% of public schools reported trouble filling at least one non-teaching position, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. That means the kids who rely on them the most are the ones who lose out when they leave or the positions can’t be filled.

The NEA ESP Bill of Rights lays out what these professionals need to stay in the jobs our kids depend on. Developed by ESPs themselves, it asks for pay that covers the bills without a second job, health care they can afford and a workplace ‘free of violence, including physical, verbal, and emotional abuse.’ It’s a practical document about what it takes to keep these jobs filled. The full list includes:.

Since the movement began, 18 states have launched ESP Bill of Rights campaigns, according to NEA.

American Education Week runs November 16 to 20, 2026, and this year NEA is using it to honor education support staff. Here are a few ways to show up for the people who show up for our kids:.

In a recent development, our kids won’t remember most of what happened at school, but they’ll remember who was kind to them there. For a lot of them, that’s a nurse, a cafeteria staff or a bus driver doing the job on less than a living wage. Sign the ESP Bill of Rights pledge and help them stay.

They say that shopping for dads is difficult. We ask: How so? We are a demographic that is easy to flatter and easy to please. If you think of us enough to buy us something, you’re 90% of the way there. And that last 10%? OK, that’s the tough part. How do you get us a gift that is unique and useful, something we’ll not just like but actually love? You’ve come to the right place.

For our 2026 list of the best gifts for dads, we’ve curated products that we know and love, ones we can say with confidence stand out from the rest of the pack. And yeah, there are a few things on this list that we just think are cool — because why not? We guarantee you’ll find something here to make him — or yourself — smile, smell good, look good, or feel cool.

According to recent reports, every product you see here is independently selected by our editors, writers, and experts. If you click a link on our site and buy something, we may earn an affiliate commission.

A dull knife is a dangerous knife. This two-sided cylindrical sharpener is a great way to keep your blades in working order. Secure your knife at the correct angle with the included magnetic holder and roll the cylinder — which has two sides, one meant for blade sharpening and one meant for honing — back and forth against the knife’s edge. Simple. Effective. The kit comes with a sharpener, strop, magnetic holder, and a display.

Recent findings suggest that A baseball cap can do more than cover up a missed shower. Siegelman Stable makes the sort you put on deliberately. The Newly introduced York label has fans like Knicks star Jalen Brunson, but there's nothing shouty about its classic shape and embroidered logo. Wear it with a jacket that fits and sneakers that aren't falling apart, and suddenly school pickup doesn't look like the end of a very long day.

According to recent reports, A cashmere blazer sounds like the sort of thing you wear to complain about the service on a yacht. This one is more useful. Quince cuts it from 100 percent Mongolian cashmere, then adds horn buttons and a partial lining for just enough structure. It wears like a sweater but looks like he made an effort. Throw it over a T-shirt and he's ready for dinner without having to change into something stiff.

Industry observers note that there are pants that look good and pants you can comfortably wear on a six-hour flight. Vuori's Meta Pant manages both. The classic five-pocket silhouette looks polished enough for the office or dinner, but the four-way stretch, moisture-wicking fabric, and quick-drying finish make them considerably more forgiving than ordinary trousers. The straight-leg fit leaves room through the hips and thighs without looking baggy.

In a recent development, one pair of boots for a rainy commute, a weekend away, and dinner somewhere nice. That's the argument for Blundstone's Heritage #156. Premium black leather keeps them sharp, cushioned footbeds and cork filler make them increasingly comfortable, and Goodyear welt construction means the soles can be replaced. They don't need babying or a special outfit. A rare thing: shoes that get more useful as they get older.

Vitamix, the most storied brand in blenders, is becoming a bit more portable. The latest Nano blends two 20-ounce cups — complete with travel lids — so that you can make a smoothie in the morning, saving your big, overpowered Vitamix for more heavy-duty food prep.

A man's wallet shouldn't resemble a filing cabinet. Bellroy's Hide & Seek keeps things slim without forcing him to give up cash, cards, or the occasional receipt he's convinced he'll need someday. Made from supple leather, the classic bifold has five card slots, a bill compartment, and concealed pockets for anything he'd rather keep tucked away. The Everglade green is particularly good, a welcome departure from the usual black and brown.

According to recent reports, men's jewelry doesn't have to involve leather cords, nautical hardware, or anything resembling a guitar pick. Mejuri's Braided Curb Chain Bracelet keeps things simple, with interwoven stainless-steel links and a sleek platinum-colored finish. It has enough presence to look intentional without becoming the centerpiece of his outfit. Water-resistant and durable enough for everyday wear, it works equally well with a T-shirt or a tailored jacket.

In a recent development, ian McEwan’s latest novel proves this is the golden age for sci-fi dystopian. While the flooded, fragmented future laid out in the book shows 2119 to be a bit of a horror show, the scholars reminiscence for art, love, and lost chance in 2014 is equal parts chilling, moving, and full of hope. .

Steve McQueen wore Persol 714s. That's a pretty compelling endorsement, even six decades later. The Italian-made frames fold into a compact shape, with rich acetate and discreet metal detailing that have survived more fashion cycles than most sunglasses ever will. No oversize logos, no aggressive wraparound lenses. Just an excellent pair of shades for a man whose taste hasn't been entirely surrendered to practical footwear.

According to recent reports, some coffee-table books are glorified furniture. This one earns its space. Architectural Digest at 100 opens the doors to a century of remarkable homes, from those of David Bowie and Truman Capote to Barack and Michelle Obama. You'll also find work by Frank Lloyd Wright, Frank Gehry, and other design heavyweights. The photography is gorgeous, but the real draw is seeing how people with extraordinary taste actually lived. For the dad who notices the architecture before he notices the menu.

Yes, it's a notebook. A very good one. Leuchtturm1917 gives him 251 numbered pages, a table of contents, two ribbon markers, and binding that lies flat without a wrestling match. It's the place for the business idea, the sketch, the travel strategy, or the novel he's been threatening to write. No apps, passwords, or notifications. Just paper substantial enough to make him want to use it.

In a recent development, the Sabah lives in the sweet spot between a loafer and a slipper, without looking much like either. Handmade in Turkey, the Blackout version pairs soft black leather with hand stitching, a leather insole that shapes to his foot, and a replaceable rubber outsole. Wear it with trousers, shorts or whatever passes for his weekend uniform. It's the sort of relaxed, distinctive shoe you notice precisely because it isn't trying so hard.

Most headphones are anonymous plastic. Nothing's Headphone (1) Pro looks like someone actually thought about the design. Behind the striking shell are three drivers, adaptive noise cancellation, and tuning developed with Metropolis Studios. Real buttons and dials mean less fumbling at the earcups, while the battery runs up to 68 hours with noise cancellation off. For a dad who's spent enough time listening to other people's playlists, here's a way back to his own.

Recent findings suggest that it has a tuning dial. An actual dial. Tivoli's Model One is a gorgeous antidote to the idea that every piece of technology needs an app and a setup tutorial. The wood cabinet, simple knobs, and traditional AM/FM radio make it a pleasure to use, while Bluetooth is there when he wants to stream something. Set it on a desk or bookshelf. Turn it on. Listen. Remember when that was all it took?

Marshall's Minor IV earbuds have a little of the brand's old-school amplifier swagger, minus the equipment truck. The black-and-gold finish is sharp, the angled design is made for a comfortable fit, and touch controls handle music and calls. Battery life runs up to seven hours per charge and more than 30 with the case. They're water-resistant, too. A solid upgrade for the dad who still cares what comes through his headphones, even if he now listens at a more reasonable volume.

In a recent development, if he has opinions about beans, water temperature, and extraction times, he needs a grinder that can keep up. Fellow's Opus 2 handles everything from espresso to cold brew, with fine grind adjustments and 48-millimeter conical burrs. Anti-static technology cuts down on the mess, and magnetic catch cups make switching methods simple. The sleek profile doesn't hurt. But the point isn't the countertop aesthetic. It's better coffee before any guests start asking where their shoes are.

In a recent development, this year’s Booker prize winner is a dystopian sci-fi satire that takes place up and down the British coast. It’s not exactly a beach read, but a novel that is a perfectly odd reflection of our perfectly strange times.

According to recent reports, A slab of teak isn't an obvious gift until you see this one. Sonder LA's Bradbury board has three compartments for chopped ingredients or a serious cheese spread. Turn it over and a deep groove catches up to 4.5 ounces of carving juices, saving the counter from the aftermath of Sunday dinner. Heavy, handsome, and useful enough to leave out all the time. It's the cutting board version of buying one good thing instead of three mediocre ones.

Smithey's cast-iron chef skillet looks like something a grandparent might have handed down, except this one comes ready to start its own history. The polished interior develops seasoning over time, the curved sides make tossing food easier, and the weight holds heat beautifully for searing. It's made in South Carolina and looks good enough to bring straight to the table. For the dad who finds chopping onions therapeutic and considers a well-seasoned pan a point of pride.

It has been revealed that A drawer full of knives is no substitute for one excellent one. Made In's 8-inch chef knife is forged in Thiers, France, by a fifth-generation bladesmith, with a full-tang construction that gives it balance and control. It can mince herbs, chop vegetables, and tackle the Sunday roast without switching tools. The best part is how often he'll use it. Unlike most expensive kitchen gifts, this won't spend its life on display.

Finding a night when everyone's free is now the hardest part of poker. Mark & Graham takes care of everything else: two decks of cards, 100 chips, and a pebbled-leather case lined in suede. It's compact enough to put away but handsome enough not to. Add a monogram if he likes that sort of thing. Then put an evening on the calendar and let him spend a few hours with people who don't need help finding their cleats.

No sprawling backyard? No problem. Solo Stove's Mesa XL brings a real flame to a compact tabletop fire pit, with an airflow system that helps keep smoke down. The stainless-steel body looks good on a patio, and the setup is simple enough for an impromptu evening outside. Roast marshmallows with the kids or pull up chairs after bedtime. It's a small fire with an outsized ability to make an ordinary Tuesday feel like something else.

The mind of the famous neurologist Oliver Sacks was like no other. His letters show his thoughts in full light — restless, deep, and full of love and wisdom. Think of this book as competency porn — a counter to the daily doomscrolling.

Sources indicate that chess is a wonderful game, provided you enjoy being intellectually humiliated by a 12-year-old. This smart chessboard might help him even the odds. Built-in sensors track every move, while LED lights suggest what to do next, and AI-powered coaching helps players improve without enduring another smug lecture about strategy. Connect it to Chess.com or Lichess to challenge opponents around the world, play against the computer, or settle a family rivalry the old-fashioned way.

A puffer jacket for your neck sounds ridiculous until the temperature drops. Cotopaxi's Fuego Down Scarf delivers the warmth of an insulated jacket in a lightweight, packable scarf, with responsibly sourced down, a water-resistant recycled nylon shell, and bold color-blocked stripes. A pull-through slit keeps it securely in place, while pockets at either end give Dad somewhere to warm his hands when gloves aren't enough.

Sources indicate that A leisurely hike is one thing. Scrambling up a rocky trail and navigating a steep descent is another. Leki's Makalu Cork Lite trekking poles give Dad some extra stability when the terrain gets tricky, without weighing him down. Made from lightweight aluminum, each pole weighs less than 9 ounces and has an ergonomic cork grip that absorbs moisture and gradually conforms to his hand. Adjustable locking mechanisms make it easy to change the length on the go, while carbide tips provide traction on uneven ground. They telescope down for packing, too.

Industry observers note that the nightstand looks like a cable graveyard. Anker's MagStand gives it a chance at redemption, charging three devices with a magnetic pad for compatible iPhones, a retractable USB-C cable, and another USB-C port. A small display demonstrates charging status and other information, while a quieter overnight mode suits a bedroom. It's the sort of unglamorous upgrade that feels extremely glamorous the first time he reaches for a fully charged phone and doesn't pull a nest of wires off the table.

Recent findings suggest that for the Formula 1 dad with extremely confident opinions about tire strategy. Logitech's McLaren racing bundle pairs an F1-style wheel with direct-drive force feedback, so the steering pushes back as traction and cornering forces change in the game. It's far closer to a simulator than a standard controller, and requires the space and enthusiasm to match. A serious indulgence, yes. But probably less expensive than any other way of letting him pretend he's on the grid.

Sources indicate that at some point in your parenting adventures, whether you like it or not, you will have to face the trials and tribulations of what it means to be a teenager. This book deeply, and sometimes even profoundly, explores just this, with equal parts science and storytelling, it might not help you truly prepare for your little one to hit their pubescence, but it will give you empathy and maybe even a bit of appreciation.

It has been revealed that keys jangle, scratch phones, and vanish precisely when everyone is late. Orbitkey stacks three to seven of them inside a slim leather organizer, then adds a tracker that works with Apple Find My or Google Find Hub on compatible devices. It takes less room in a pocket and looks considerably better than a bulky ring. Not the showiest gift here. Possibly the one he'll use most often.

Recent findings suggest that remember when listening to music meant putting on an album and actually listening to the whole thing? The Retradisc CD player brings back that pleasure, minus the tangled headphone cords. Its transparent case lets Dad watch his CDs spin, while Bluetooth connectivity lets him pair it with wireless headphones or speakers. There's also a traditional headphone jack, anti-skip protection, and a rechargeable battery.

Industry observers note that some dads count steps. Others count elevation gain. Garmin's Enduro 4 is for the second group, with trail maps, endurance metrics, stamina tracking, and more than 100 activity profiles. Its solar-assisted battery can last up to 90 days in smartwatch mode under Garmin's specified sunlight conditions, which makes it especially useful on long trips. It's overkill for walking the dog. For someone planning his next ultramarathon before finishing the last one, that's the appeal.

He tracks workouts, sleep, and maybe his resting heart rate. Why stop at weight? Withings' BodyScan 2 measures composition by body region, tracks muscle and fat mass, and offers cardiovascular metrics including a six-lead ECG and vascular age estimates. Results appear on a screen built into the handle. Some advanced analysis requires a subscription, and it's not a replacement for a doctor. Buy it for the data enthusiast who actually wants this information, not as a hint that somebody should get in shape.

It has been revealed that the fleece vest has spent far too long being associated with finance bros who say things like “let's circle back.” It's time to reclaim it. The North Face's Glacier Vest is lightweight, warm, and made entirely from recycled polyester fleece. It's the ideal extra layer for chilly morning walks, weekend hikes, or an office where someone has apparently mistaken the thermostat for a refrigerator dial.

Sources indicate that because exercise equipment has a way of proliferating and is generally ugly, at-home workouts tend to require a sacrifice of one kind or another. The possible lone exception is the rowing machine: Rowing works 86 percent of the body’s muscles and can be as cardio-intense (or mellow) as you like, while improving joint flexibility. One of the newest and sleekest rowing machines, the Ergatta uses actual water resistance, which makes it as effective as it is quiet (as well as cool-looking, with its transparent reservoir). It’s got all the fitness potential of a traditional rowing machine, but packaged with cutting-edge, immersive technology (a reasonable $29/month) that keeps monotony at bay. The jewel in the crown, though, is its design: Handmade of cherry wood, it's the farthest thing from an eyesore, and it can be folded up and stowed away, so it works in even the tiniest of homes.

Just looking at this hammock drops your diastolic blood pressure. String this version up between two trees, or on a stand, and the generous 55-by-82-inch hammock will cradle him with an open back that prevents sweating in the summer heat. The cord is as soft as cotton, but the synthetic blend inhibits discoloration in the sun, is anti-microbial, and easy to clean with soap and water when the kids spill watermelon on it.

Sure, you can find a dozen pricey, aesthetically arresting turntables out there, but for the man who actually listens to his records, you can't beat AudioTechnica. The biggest upgrade for a vinyl spin is found in the manual turntable and the seemingly no-frills AT-LPW30 puts all the focus on great sound and proper listening experience.

He may be shaving in a hurry, but the products don't have to feel like a compromise. Le Labo pairs a rich shaving cream with a soothing after-shave balm in minimalist aluminum tubes. Bergamot, lavender, violet, and tonka bean give the set a distinctive scent without the usual blast of drugstore aftershave. It turns a boring morning task into something a little more civilized. No 10-step ritual required.

It has been revealed that A beautiful fresh edition of William Gibson's seminal 1984 cyberpunk novel. Illustrated throughout by Anna Mill, with a handsome slipcase.

Sources indicate that aventus is not a subtle little stocking stuffer. It's Creed's big, unapologetically luxurious fragrance, with fresh bergamot and blackcurrant giving way to pineapple, pink pepper, and smoky birch. The mix feels rich without veering into syrupy. Yes, the price is extravagant. That's rather the point. For a dad who's particular about fragrance and rarely buys the expensive bottle for himself, this is a proper splurge.

In a recent development, if the household has a snorer, a restless sleeper, or a neighbor who enjoys late-night construction projects, these might be the most welcome gift of the season. Ozlo's Sleepbuds 2 sit low in the ear, including for side sleepers, and play sleep sounds to help mask noise. They can also stream music or podcasts, with up to 14 hours of battery life and a private in-ear alarm. The case monitors bedroom conditions, too. They can't make anyone sleep later. They might make the hours he gets a little quieter.

Dad's face has been through a lot. Early mornings, late nights, questionable sleep, and possibly decades of washing it with whatever soap happens to be in the shower. It deserves better. Caldera + Lab's The Regimen gives him a proper skin care routine without requiring a degree in dermatology. The four-piece set includes a gentle exfoliating cleanser, a botanical serum, a daily moisturizer, and an eye treatment designed to tackle the appearance of puffiness and dark circles.

Industry observers note that some people throw out a broken gadget. Others want to see exactly what's gone wrong inside. iFixit's Mako kit is for the latter, with 64 precision bits for laptops, game consoles, phones, and the obscure screws that defeat an ordinary screwdriver. The aluminum driver has a magnetic socket and swivel top; the case keeps everything from scattering across the table. A small, deeply satisfying gift for the dad who believes almost anything deserves one attempt at repair.

It has been revealed that the moment you become a dad, people start assuming you can fix things. Leatherman's Wingman won't supply the expertise, but it gives him 14 ways to look prepared. Spring-action pliers, scissors, screwdrivers, wire cutters, a blade, and a package opener all fold into one pocketable tool. The knife opens with one hand and the 25-year warranty suggests it's meant to stick around. One of those gifts he'll reach for long after the holidays are forgotten.

According to recent reports, flat-pack furniture has destroyed more relationships than anyone cares to admit. Hoto's PivotDrive won't save a marriage, but it might prevent an argument over a bookshelf. This sleek cordless screwdriver has a head that pivots 90 degrees, with four locking positions to reach screws buried in tight corners and awkward spaces. Five torque settings, two speeds, and 16 interchangeable bits handle everything from furniture assembly to minor household repairs. It's a clever upgrade for the guy who enjoys fixing things almost as much as complaining about how badly they were designed.

Drinks You Can Make By The Batch

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Holiday magic is a lot of unpaid labor in an ugly Christmas sweater.
  • Recent findings suggest that these punches, pitchers and alcohol-free drinks are perfect for pre-proposal prepping.There’s a spicy margarita you can carry in the tequila bottle, a pear punch for the fancy friends, and a peppermint espresso martini you can make for 16.
  • Julie Reiner, co-founder of Brooklyn’s Clover Club, served punch and freezer cocktails at a Halloween party for 20.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bring something good. Let the grown-ups serve themselves.

Holiday magic is a lot of unpaid labor in an ugly Christmas sweater. Between class potlucks, Thanksgiving logistics and buying the only bread your kid will eat, you’ve got enough on your plate. Now add holiday parties, questionable white elephant gifts and 400 things to do before the doorbell rings. The last thing you need is a second job as a bartender.

Recent findings suggest that these punches, pitchers and alcohol-free drinks are perfect for pre-proposal prepping.There’s a spicy margarita you can carry in the tequila bottle, a pear punch for the fancy friends, and a peppermint espresso martini you can make for 16. Some need a little attention before serving. Most are ready to pour once chilled.

Julie Reiner, co-founder of Brooklyn’s Clover Club, served punch and freezer cocktails at a Halloween party for 20. “The goal is to spend time with your guests, not be stuck behind the bar all night!” she stated.

A little planning helps. Julianna McIntosh, the cocktail creator behind Join Jules, recommends using fresh citrus the day of your party and accounting for the water normally added when you shake or stir a drink with ice. Hannah Chamberlain, the recipe developer behind Spirited LA, has another rule: Hold the ice and bubbly until guests arrive. Otherwise, you risk a watered-down punch with flat bubbles.

Bringing a batch to someone else’s party? Pack it in a tightly sealed container, keep it chilled and add the bubbles when you arrive. Then pour yourself a glass and let someone else worry about the rest.

According to recent reports, bitter, bubbly and ridiculously easy to scale up. Natalie Migliarini, the cocktail creator behind Beautiful Booze, makes her Negroni Sbagliato with equal parts Select Aperitivo, sweet vermouth and prosecco, finished with an orange slice. The recipe makes one, but you can multiply the aperitivo and vermouth to serve your group, then chill them together in a bottle. When it's time to drink, pour over ice, add the prosecco and stir. No shaker required.

Get the recipe at Beautiful Booze.

Sources indicate that everyone’s due at six. The first guest rings the bell at 5:42. Have Reiner’s Boat House Punch ready. Gin, Aperol, St-Germain and three citrus juices get a bright, bittersweet lift from sparkling rosé. “I always want my punch to be a crowd-pleaser, but it needs to have a little personality too!” Reiner remarked. This makes a substantial batch, so save it for a crowd. Let the lemon peels and sugar sit for at least an hour or overnight, and freeze a large ice block ahead of time. Add the ice and rosé just before serving.

Get the recipe at Cocktails Distilled.

Recent findings suggest that champagne tastes even better when nobody has to mix 12 individual cocktails. Chamberlain's large-batch take on the French 75 combines gin, fresh lemon, orange bitters and homemade cranberry-ginger syrup, then gets topped with sparkling wine. It serves six to eight and looks impressive without requiring an elaborate garnish situation. Make the syrup ahead and chill the ingredients. When guests arrive, add large ice cubes and the bubbly, give it a stir, and you're done. If the finished punch tastes a little dull, Chamberlain recommends adding a few dashes of Angostura or cardamom bitters to give it more personality.

In a recent development, love your friends. Not enough to muddle each of them a mojito. Averie Sunshine’s pomegranate mojito punch at Averie Cooks combines white rum, mint, pomegranate juice and seeds, lemon and sparkling water in one pitcher. It makes four generous drinks, so double it for a bigger gathering. Chill the liquids ahead, then muddle the mint and assemble the punch just before serving so the leaves stay fresh, and the bubbles don't disappear. Ice goes in the glasses. One round of muddling. Everybody gets a drink.

Get the recipe at Averie Cooks.

According to recent reports, here, Chamberlain pairs pear nectar with gin, ginger liqueur, rosemary syrup, lemon, cardamom bitters and dry bubbly in her Calling Card Punch. It's an elegant, herbal alternative to the usual holiday punch and serves six to eight. Make the rosemary syrup ahead, chill the ingredients and add the sparkling wine while serving.

Sources indicate that “I tend to build my punch a little less sweet and then I’ll often have a little extra syrup I can add if it seems unbalanced,” Chamberlain stated. It's easier to add sweetness than take it away.

By the time dessert rolls around, the adults deserve something stronger than another cup of coffee. McIntosh combines vodka, espresso or cold brew, coffee liqueur and peppermint syrup for a holiday spin on the espresso martini. Her large-batch version makes about 16 servings, with no individual shaking required. Mix everything ahead, chill it in the freezer for about two hours and give it a quick whirl in the blender if you want that signature foam. Pour into a punch bowl and let everyone help themselves. Crushed candy cane rims are optional. You've already done enough decorating.

Give the alcohol-free drinks their own spot at the party. America’s Test Kitchen combines cranberries, ginger, rosemary, cinnamon and star anise in a sweetened base you can make up to four days ahead. When guests arrive, add chilled cranberry juice, orange juice and seltzer. It makes 16 servings, enough for an open house where another family keeps appearing in the doorway.

Get the recipe at America’s Test Kitchen.

According to recent reports, the tiny apple leaves are optional – you have enough crafts coming home from school. Chamberlain’s Fallen Leaves Punch mixes cognac, tart apple cider and lemon with homemade cranberry-cinnamon syrup for eight servings. It's a good Friendsgiving option if you want something tart, fruity and a little stronger than cider.

“In terms of flavor combinations, it’s hard to disappoint with the combination of seasonal spice and fruit,” Chamberlain stated. Make the syrup ahead, squeeze the lemons the day of and stir everything over a large ice block at serving.

Industry observers note that taco night doesn’t need a November makeover. McIntosh makes six spicy margaritas right in the tequila bottle, giving you a batch and a carrying container in one. You'll need to pour out some tequila first; the recipe tells you how much. Mix everything in the bottle, then let it sit in the freezer for 2 to 4 hours, then pour it over ice into salt-rimmed glasses. All the fun of margaritas without anyone spending the evening squeezing limes.

It has been revealed that apple cider is doing a lot of heavy lifting this holiday season, let it have some rum. Chamberlain's Cider Rum Punch combines tart cider, aged pineapple rum, lemon, orange bitters and a homemade mulling-spice syrup for six servings. She makes it every year, and it's easy to see why. The warm spices play nicely with the fruit without turning the whole thing into a scented candle. Make the syrup ahead, then combine everything in a pitcher with plenty of ice and stir until chilled. Bonus: There's no sparkling wine to worry about going flat.

The kids’ table and Grandma can drink from the same pitcher. McIntosh’s pineapple passion fruit agua fresca blends tropical fruit, lime and agave into six refreshing alcohol-free servings. Frozen passion fruit pulp works, and there are no bubbles to go flat on the drive. Make it up to two days ahead, refrigerate and give it a good stir before pouring over ice.

After the holiday lights walk, everyone comes home freezing and suddenly needs something warm RIGHT NOW. Sunshine's peppermint white hot chocolate at Averie Cooks combines milk, melted white chocolate and a little peppermint extract. The recipe makes five mugs, but you can easily double or triple it for a houseful of cold kids and grown-ups. Heat everything together over low heat, stirring until the chocolate melts. Don't let it boil, and go easy on the peppermint. A little goes a long way. Add marshmallows if you've got them. Nobody's going to complain.

Get the recipe at Averie Cooks.

Sources indicate that the wine people and the margarita people can share a pitcher. Migliarini’s tequila sangria at Beautiful Booze combines Sauvignon Blanc with tequila, cranberry syrup, fresh cranberries, red and green apples and lime. “Keeping it simple, my recipe includes fruits that are available throughout the entire year,” she writes in the recipe. It serves five to six, making it a good choice for a casual Friendsgiving. Chill the wine, tequila and fruit mixture ahead, then add the lemon-lime soda just before serving.

Get the recipe at Beautiful Booze.

In a recent development, no fish. Promise. Amy Traynor’s Fish House Punch at Moody Mixologist combines cognac and aged rum with peach liqueur, lemon and cold black tea. Think peach iced tea with considerably more going on. Her recipe includes a version for 10, so there's no need to multiply or do any guesswork. Freeze a large ice block ahead, stir the ingredients over it at serving and finish each glass with freshly grated nutmeg. Fair warning: This one's boozy.

Get the recipe at Moody Mixologist.

Recent findings suggest that dinner’s over, the kids have claimed the television and nobody’s ready to leave. Put a pot of McIntosh’s mulled Aperol on the stove for the spritz drinkers still on your sofa. Dry white wine, Aperol, apple cider and honey warm with orange and whole spices. It makes six servings and needs just 15 to 20 minutes over low heat. Don't let it boil. Ladle into mugs and let everyone settle in. The kitchen will smell like you had a initiative.

  • I talked with two physicians who’ve treated these kids, Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

E-bikes and e-scooters have become a hot item on holiday and birthday wish lists. They’ve also become a hot topic in online forums and parenting circles, where people constantly worry about kids on e-bikes going too fast, losing control or making poor choices. I’ve seen it myself on my city’s bike path—kids flying by and recklessly weaving past pedestrians and other cyclists.

Sources indicate that if you’re trying to decide whether or not to give your kid an e-bike, it helps to know what pediatricians are seeing in their emergency rooms. A JAMA study published in November 2026 looked at more than 13,000 injury visits for kids under 18 at six large U.S. children’s hospitals between 2023 and early 2026. E-bike injuries grew 33% per quarter over that stretch and e-scooter injuries grew 15% per quarter, compared with 2% for traditional bikes and 4% for traditional scooters. About a quarter of the e-bike injuries and nearly half of the e-scooter injuries involved kids under 12.

I talked with two physicians who’ve treated these kids, Dr. Beth C. Natt, system medical director of pediatrics at Atlantic Health, and Dr. Zebulon J. Timmons, division chief of emergency medicine at Children’s Nebraska in Omaha, about what parents should weigh before buying one and how to keep kids safer if one is already in the garage.

Recent findings suggest that “It mostly comes down to speed,” Natt says. “Doubling the speed roughly quadruples the force in a crash.” Some e-bikes can top 25 mph, and Natt notes that e-bike crashes are far more likely to involve a car.

Timmons points to the rider as much as the bike. “Kids do not have the frontal lobe capacity and reaction time to make judgments at that speed,” he claims. “You don’t take your young child to the batting cages and have them start at 80 mph.”.

It has been revealed that in the JAMA study, 17% of e-bike injuries led to a hospital stay, the highest share of any group of injuries, and 10% involved a brain injury, double the rate for regular bikes. Severe injuries, like those needing ICU care or surgery to fix a fracture, were twice as common on e-bikes, too (8% vs. 4%). Natt mostly sees broken wrists, arms and legs, plus head, face and dental injuries. Timmons sees a lot of open fractures, where the bone breaks through the skin. “Kids’ heads are bigger relative to their bodies, so they tend to hit head-first,” Natt says, “and a fracture through a growth plate can affect how a bone grows later.”.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) claims kids under 16 shouldn’t ride e-scooters and, citing Consumer Product Safety Commission guidance, no e-bikes for kids under 12. Timmons says kids 12 to 15 can ride a Class 1 e-bike with proper safety training and gear, and teens 16 and up can consider a Class 2, though many will still be safer on a Class 1. Natt is more conservative. “Most pediatric injury experts would say no throttle-powered e-bike or e-scooter before about 16, and some argue for 18,” she says.

A child is ready, Natt claims, if they can handle a regular bike confidently in traffic, follow the rules when you’re not around, wear a helmet without reminders and judge how fast cars are coming. “Most kids don’t have that judgment until at least their teens,” she notes.

Class 1 e-bikes are pedal-assist only, up to 20 mph. Class 2 adds a throttle, still capped at 20 mph. Class 3 is pedal-assist up to 28 mph, and many states restrict it to riders 16 and older. For kids, choose Class 1 and skip the throttle, Natt notes, and avoid “e-motos” sold as e-bikes, since they go much faster. Both doctors note a regular pedal bike is still the safest choice for most kids.

There’s no federal minimum age for e-bikes, and more than half of states set age limits for Class 3 models, so check your state and town’s rules before you buy.

Timmons notes a standard bike helmet is fine up to about 15 mph. From 15 to 25 mph, he recommends a helmet certified to the NTA 8776 e-bike standard, and above 25 mph, a motorcycle or moped helmet. A full-face helmet adds protection for the face and jaw, Natt says, and any helmet should be replaced after a crash.

Keeping it on is another matter. Timmons claims fewer than 25% of kids treated in pediatric emergency departments were wearing a helmet when they crashed, and many take them off once they’re out of a parent’s sight. Make wearing a helmet a non-negotiable, and let friends and neighbors know to keep an eye on your child. If they’re spotted without the helmet, the bike goes away.

Recent findings suggest that after the helmet, wrist guards and gloves help most because broken wrists are so common, Natt indicates. Front and rear lights plus reflective clothing help drivers see your child. Timmons recommends that kids wear closed-toe shoes (“No Crocs”), and for teens 16 and up on a Class 2, motorcycle-style long pants and sleeves.

Sources indicate that any head injury or neck pain after an e-bike or e-scooter crash should be checked in the emergency room, Timmons says. Natt says to go if your child passed out, even briefly, or keeps vomiting, or has a worsening headache, confusion, unusual sleepiness, a seizure, weakness or numbness, belly pain, a limb that looks bent or can’t bear weight, or a deep cut or facial or dental injury.

In a recent development, watch for “handlebar injuries,” too, when the handlebars turn sideways and strike the chest or belly. “This mechanism causes all the force to be delivered to a small area and can cause significant internal injuries,” Timmons claims. A handlebar-shaped bruise on the chest or abdomen means a trip to the ER. Once there, tell the care team what kind of e-bike your child was riding and whether they wore a helmet, Natt says.

If the e-bike or e-scooter isn’t right for your child’s age, consider exchanging it, Timmons states, or look for a community buy-back program. “This last trauma season was the worst one in my career and that was largely driven by e-bike/scooter injuries,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that “These are motor vehicles, not toys,” Natt says. “A crash at e-bike speed can look more like a motorcycle injury than a bike injury.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a subgroup of the World Health Organization, will make the official announcement today.

According to recent reports, measles has made headlines time and time again over the past two years, as cases have hit record highs and vaccination rates have reached record lows. Now, the looming threat has come true: according to sources familiar with the vote, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) revoked the United States’ measles elimination status.

The group is expected to make a formal announcement today.

To date, the U.S. has racked up more than 5,400 confirmed measles cases in 2026, the most to be reported in the United States in 35 years. There have been 10 reported measles-related deaths so far, including an infant in Wisconsin earlier this month. Measles was considered officially eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, meaning there had been no large outbreaks or uncontrolled domestic transmission of the virus for at least 12 months prior.

According to recent reports, america’s current measles outbreaks first began in January 2025 in West Texas. By January 2026, the spread continued unchecked. PAHO’s meeting to discuss the country’s measles elimination status was originally scheduled for April 2026, KFF reports, but the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) asked for more time to determine whether measles cases were being transmitted domestically or “imported” (for example, if someone contracted measles abroad and then brought it to the U.S.). According to NBC, measles is now considered endemic to the U.S.

Recent findings suggest that many concerns have contributed to the country’s ongoing measles outbreaks, from sweeping funding and staffing cuts to public health agencies to a lack of leadership — there was no Senate-confirmed director of the CDC for an entire year during this measles outbreak. But the main driver is declining vaccination rates, which experts blame on the Trump administration, specifically HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, as Scary Mommy previously reported.

The CDC and American Academy of Pediatrics both recommend children get their first measles vaccine dose between 12 and 15 months of age, and the second dose between 4 and 6 years of age before starting school. According to CDC data, 96% of measles cases in 2026 have occurred in unvaccinated individuals. A KFF poll found that roughly one in five adults believe getting the measles vaccine is more dangerous than becoming infected with the measles. Parents are commonly exposed to vaccine misinformation, and data demonstrates it is affecting their health decisions: the number of kindergarteners with vaccine exemptions rose to 4.2% in the 2025-2026 school year, the highest in the country’s history, with 39 states falling below the 95% vaccinated threshold needed to prevent outbreaks.

“The expected loss of America’s status as having eradicated measles will be a tragedy because it reflects the preventable loss of human lives. It is unthinkable that people in the United States should be dying from measles in 2026,” mentioned Wendy S. Armstrong, M.D., president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, in a publicly issued statement. “Our government’s leaders and public health officials must heed this urgent warning and take actions that slow the spread. That starts with promoting vaccination against measles, which is proven to be safe and effective.”.

The largest outbreak in the U.S. since it earned measles elimination status, prior to the current one, was in 2018-2019. It was curtailed through a strong federal and state-level public health response, including closing schools where transmission occurred, prohibiting unvaccinated children from attending school, and fining parents for not vaccinating their children, KFF reports. The CDC also declared a public health emergency and made “clear statements about the importance of measles vaccinations.”.

Recent findings suggest that but last week, CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz told Reuters that the agency will not make any major changes to their handling of the outbreak regardless of PAHO’s decision. The CDC will continue to “help [the states] provide awareness about ​measles, emphasizing, reemphasizing that the number one way to prevent measles is the MMR (combined measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine,” she said.

She attributed the ongoing spread of measles to “closely knit communities” — several outbreaks have started in religious communities, like among the Pennsylvania Amish, where vaccination rates are lower than other parts of the country.

“These communities typically don’t vaccinate their children...their families were making decisions about the MMR vaccine 20 to 30 years ago and we’re just now seeing the results of those decisions,” Schwartz noted.

According to recent reports, in response, the AAP and nearly 150 other health care organizations published a letter calling on Kennedy Jr. and Schwartz to develop and implement a plan to eliminate measles in the United States. Their recommendations include restoring evidence-based immunization policies, proactively encouraging measles vaccination, and conveying accurate information about measles and MMR vaccines.
