Waxing and waning signs, vague symptoms that come and go. A cat that is on deathâs door one moment, running around the next. Detecting illness in cats can be difficult enough, but when the body starts attacking itself, diagnosis becomes even more of a challenge.

In an autoimmune disease, a catâs immune system malfunctions and begins attacking the body it is meant to protect. Fortunately, autoimmune disease is relatively uncommon in cats, but it can be serious and difficult to diagnose and treat. Because the signs tend to be vague and can come and go, they are easy to overlook, which makes it worth knowing what to watch for and when to involve a vet.

A healthy immune system protects the body from germs such as viruses and bacteria by sending out specialized cells to locate and destroy them. It also helps clear away damaged or diseased cells. These immune cells use protein signals on the surface of the bodyâs own cells to recognize them as safe. In autoimmune disease, a signaling error causes the immune system to treat the catâs own cells as a threat, and healthy, working tissue gets attacked and destroyed.

It has been revealed that cats can develop these problems much as people do. They can affect any part of the body, including the internal organs, blood, and skin, and there are many different types. Some can be life-threatening, weakening the bodyâs natural defenses while also damaging healthy tissue.

Industry observers note that the part of the body under attack determines which signs appear, so the picture varies dramatically from one cat to the next. Signs are often general and not immediately linked to an autoimmune problem. Possible signs include lethargy, weakness, decreased appetite, weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, and other changes to the feces. Other signs include pale gums, unexplained bleeding, bruising, a high temperature, a faster heart rate, rapid breathing, and tiring easily during play. Limping, swollen joints, sores on the skin, a poor coat, increased thirst, increased urination, and collapse are also on the list.

Many of these signs come and go. A cat may seem completely fine one day and be struggling the next. Any of these signs are a reason to contact a vet promptly, since starting investigations early makes a real difference.

Sources indicate that the problem starts with the catâs own immune system, which is part of what makes it so hard to manage. The exact triggers are not fully understood, and more research is needed. An immune-mediated condition can be triggered when the immune system is stimulated. Viral infections, vaccination, medications, inherited conditions, and hormones have all been linked to autoimmune disease. Where things get tricky is that the incident that triggered the disease is not usually the cause of the disease. That means that the same type of autoimmune disease can be triggered by different things in different individuals.

Industry observers note that some of these conditions can be passed down, and other possible contributors include poor nutrition, toxins, cancer, and stress. A cat diagnosed with an autoimmune disease considered hereditary should not be bred under any circumstances.

According to recent reports, diagnosis is often a process of elimination. More common causes of the same signs are investigated and ruled out first, which can mean lots of tests. A vet will start with a full physical exam and a detailed history, then choose tests to fit the signs. These may include blood and urine tests, X-rays, or an ultrasound scan. Samples may also be taken from wounds, rashes, or other affected areas. Prompt diagnosis is vital for effective management.

Treatment depends on the type of autoimmune disease, what part of the body is affected, and what is behind it, so it varies greatly. The usual approach is medication that calms the immune system so it stops attacking the body, most often corticosteroids like prednisone or dexamethasone. A large starting dose is often given, and once the signs settle down, the dose is lowered gradually.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes, stronger immunosuppressive drugs are also used. Some of them are also used in cancer treatment, and the side effects tend to be more severe. The trouble with treating an immune-mediated disease is that we are using medication to suppress the immune system, and that leaves the patient more susceptible to infection and other diseases.

Even more challenging when treating feline autoimmune disease is that some of the medications used to treat dogs or humans are toxic to cats.

Supportive care matters just as much. Pain relief is often needed, but many commonly prescribed anti-inflammatory painkillers cannot be given alongside steroids. Stronger painkillers like opioids or gabapentin may be used to manage severe pain, and these come with their own side effects. Antibiotics may also be prescribed, either prophylactically if extremely high doses of immunosuppressive medications are being used, or if secondary infections develop.

For cats with immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA), where the immune system is attacking and destroying red blood cells, or immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (IMTP) where platelets are being destroyed, blood or plasma transfusions may be needed to save a catâs life.

It has been revealed that lifestyle changes can help too. A cat with painful, swollen joints, for example, benefits from losing weight if overweight, and lower sides on litter trays and softer beds make life more comfortable. Each case is assessed individually.

Industry observers note that one of the more common autoimmune diseases in cats is known as Eosinophilic Granuloma Complex, a group of idiopathic conditions that are currently quite poorly understood. The exact cause of the disease is unknown; however, parasites, allergies, and genetic factors have been identified as likely triggers.

There are three main clinical presentations of eosinophilic granuloma complex:.

Ulcerative: Also known as indolent ulcers or rodent ulcers, this form of eosinophilic granuloma complex usually presents with a sore on the cat's mouth. It is typically seen on the upper lip. They are normally red in color and do not appear to cause your cat any pain or irritation.

Plaque-forming: often found on the stomach and on the inside of the hind legs. The lesions are often itchy and red and often become infected, which complicates matters.

Granuloma forming: usually presents as raised pink or yellow nodules that can be located anywhere on your cat.

Another more common feline immune-mediated disease is called pemphigus foliaceus. It affects the skin, causing scabs, crusts, and sores around the eyes and ears, on the paws, and in the groin area. When it develops on the paws, the nail beds can be affected as well.

There is no cure for autoimmune disease, but effective treatment and management can control the signs, greatly improve quality of life, and allow most cats to live fairly comfortably. These conditions can be debilitating and life-threatening, yet it is often possible to manage them well enough for cats to lead relatively normal lives. Because the signs overlap with so many other conditions, a vet visit at the first sign that something is wrong is the surest way to get answers early.

When my boss passed away, I took in his older Red Heeler, Bob, so he didnât end up in the pound. I've been giving him turkey tail for his lumps, and he is overweight.

In a recent development, itâs hard to walk him when it's 100 degrees out. For the last couple of months, he has been drinking so much water and urinating way more than usual. He mostly stays inside, and when I take him out to pee, the first thing when he comes back in is head for the water bowl, like he wants to replace what he just got rid of!

Any suggestions on what I could try?â.

It has been revealed that you have done something very kind by giving Bob a home after losing his person. It sounds like he is a senior boy who has already been through a lot, and it is wonderful that he has someone looking out for him. The increased drinking and urination you are seeing, especially since this has been going on for a couple of months, is something I would have checked rather than assuming it is just his age or the hot weather. Older dogs can develop several conditions that cause this combination of signs, including diabetes, kidney disease, and Cushing's disease.

It has been revealed that I would schedule a veterinary examination and ask for some basic lab work, particularly blood tests and urinalysis. These can give us information that we simply cannot get from looking at Bob. Bloodwork can tell us about his blood glucose, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, and other changes that may help identify what is going on. A urine sample is just as valuable. It can show whether his kidneys are concentrating the urine properly, and can also detect glucose, ketones, protein, blood, inflammation, and other abnormalities. Depending on those results, his veterinarian may recommend some additional tests.

Industry observers note that please do not limit his water, even if it seems like he is drinking right back what he just urinated. In many of these conditions, the excessive thirst is the body's way of trying to replace fluid that is being lost. Taking water away can actually make him dehydrated and much sicker. Keep fresh water available at all times, and because of the heat, try to take him out during the cooler parts of the day. If you can, measuring approximately how much water he drinks in 24 hours would also be very helpful information for his veterinarian.

According to recent reports, I would also recommend that he has the lumps properly checked rather than relying on turkey tail or other supplements. Some lumps are harmless, but others can be more serious, and we cannot tell the difference just by feeling or looking at them. A fine needle aspiration can often collect cells from a lump with very little discomfort and may give the veterinarian a much better idea of what it is. With Bob being overweight and having difficulty walking in the heat, getting his medical issues sorted out first will also make it much safer to work on his weight and mobility.

He has clearly found someone who cares about him, and sometimes the most loving thing we can do for an older dog is simply to find out what his body is trying to tell us.

What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

In a recent development, that is the opportunity behind a major clinical trial from the Dog Aging Project, a research collaboration focused on giving us a better understanding of canine aging. The project is currently looking for older, healthy dogs to participate in the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs, better known as TRIAD.

This study is attracting renewed attention following a recent 60 Minutes report on the Dog Aging Project and its work investigating why dogs age the way they do and how their golden years might be made healthier.

In a recent development, TRIAD is not simply asking how long dogs can live. Researchers are trying to understand if a medication called rapamycin can influence the aging process and improve health in older dogs.

In a recent development, rapamycin, also known as sirolimus or Rapamune, is a macrolide drug with immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. This medication has been used in human medicine for more than two decades, including in patients who have undergone kidney transplantation.

Sources indicate that the interest in rapamycin and aging comes from a different area of research. Studies in laboratory organisms found that rapamycin can extend lifespan in several species, including mice, yeast, worms, and flies. Now, researchers want to find out whether those benefits could extend to our pets.

The Dog Aging Projectâs TRIAD trial is a multicenter study involving researchers and veterinary hospitals at universities across the United States, including Tufts University. The TRIAD trial is investigating whether rapamycin can influence lifespan and, importantly, promote healthy aging in companion dogs.

For veterinary science, one of the most interesting parts of aging research is the difference between lifespan and healthspan.

In a recent development, lifespan is how long an animal lives. Healthspan is the portion of that life spent in good health.

Living longer is great, but what matters just as much is how dogs feel during those extra years. More time with the family means less if a dog is struggling with chronic illness, having trouble getting around, or experiencing cognitive decline. The goal isn't just to add years to a dog's life. It's to help them enjoy more of those years feeling good.

TRIAD is examining several areas of canine health, including cognitive function, heart function, immunity, and cancer incidence.

The current TRIAD recruitment drive is specifically aimed at older dogs that meet the study's eligibility requirements. To be considered for the study, dogs must:.

Be able to cooperate with examinations, including blood collection and cardiac ultrasound, without sedation.

Have normal diagnostic findings at enrollment.

Clinical trial sites are located throughout the United States.

For families who decide to participate, it is important to consider that this is a three-year commitment. During the first year, dogs receive either rapamycin or a placebo. Once that year is over, the medication stops, but the study continues. Researchers will follow the dogs for another two years to see how they age and whether any differences emerge over time. In total, owners will bring their dogs to a clinical trial site seven times during the three-year study.

Industry observers note that when it comes to getting older, dogs and humans have quite a lot in common. Dogs are susceptible to many of the same age-related conditions we are, including cognitive decline, arthritis, heart disease, cancer, and other chronic health problems. And since they share our homes and daily environments, a great deal of what researchers learn from studying aging in dogs can be extrapolated to humans.

Recent findings suggest that the recent 60 Minutes report touched on this connection, including research into canine dementia. It's an area worth paying attention to, especially as more dogs live into their senior years.

There's also a practical advantage. Dogs age much faster than humans. This allows researchers to track changes in their health over a few years instead of waiting decades. That's a big deal when you're trying to understand what happens as the body ages.

Sources indicate that but this isn't just about what dogs can teach us about ourselves. What researchers discover will help dogs, too.

Aging isn't a single disease that can be treated with one medication. As dogs get older, several things can start changing at once, sometimes as a domino or cascade effect after an initial problem or illness. Maybe getting up becomes harder, walks get shorter, or a dog who's always been sharp seems a little confused. Sometimes these changes happen gradually, and it's easy to chalk them up to old age.

The more we learn about what's actually happening in an aging dog's body, the better chance veterinarians have of spotting problems earlier and finding ways to help dogs feel good for as long as possible.

Due to the eligibility requirements, not every dog will qualify for TRIAD, but that doesnât mean they canât contribute to canine aging research.

It has been revealed that the Dog Aging Project also has a broader research community known as the DAP Pack, which welcomes dogs of different ages, sizes, breeds, and backgrounds. The project explains that dogs who do not qualify for TRIAD can still make a meaningful contribution to understanding canine aging.

Recent findings suggest that itâs important to include all kinds of dogs in this research, not just a particular breed or size. A dog's genes, lifestyle, environment, size, and even their health history can all play a role in how they age. The more variety researchers can study, the better picture they can get of why some dogs stay healthy well into their senior years while others develop health problems earlier.

In a recent development, when it comes to canine aging, the goal isn't just to help dogs live longer. It's to help them feel good for more of those years, stay active, and keep enjoying life with their families.

And anyone who's lived with a senior dog knows that two dogs of the same age can be worlds apart. One 10-year-old may still be eager for walks, playtime, and whatever the family has planned that day. Another might be struggling with mobility or dealing with several health problems. So, what makes the difference?

Sources indicate that that's part of what makes the TRIAD study interesting. Rapamycin has shown promising results in other species, but researchers still need to find out whether it can make a meaningful difference in dogs. That's a question that needs to be tested, and your pup may be part of this!

According to recent reports, for owners of senior dogs, taking part in research like this is a chance to help scientists get some answers. What they learn could help us better understand why dogs age differently and what might help them stay healthier as they get older.

So, if you have a pup in their golden years, check out the Dog Aging Project and see how your four-legged friend might become part of this research.

In Loving Memory of Tiger

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Catster

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

This article is part two of From Misfortune to Blessing: How a Cat Lost a Leg, But Got a Forever Home.

Tiger came to my family on 2 June 2025 after an accident at a car park that resulted in his right hind leg being amputated. Before surgery, he was diagnosed with Stage B2 Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) â subclinical heart disease with a high risk of progression. We were advised to follow up on Tigerâs heart condition.

In a recent development, having incurred a high bill for his condition in 2025, we brought Tiger to a general practice vet in Singapore, not a cardiologist. It was our first time rescuing a cat, and we didnât know the difference. The vet was more concerned about Tigerâs kidneys, and during several visits in 2025, she focused on his renal function. At each visit, she would listen to Tigerâs heart with a stethoscope and tell us the condition âshould still be the sameâ. Unknown to us, Tigerâs heart condition was quietly deteriorating.

In late December 2025, we suggested to the general vet that we book an echocardiogram to scan Tigerâs heart. We had to wait for the appointment, and it finally took place on 14 February 2026.

Industry observers note that when Tiger came home from the echocardiogram, he was extremely weak. He had not eaten since midnight the previous day; the gabapentin used to relax him for the scan made him so weak that he could barely stand up, and he pooped on the floor.

The echocardiogram results took more than three weeks, and by then we were informed that Tigerâs heart condition had progressed from HCM stage B2 to congestive heart failure. Our vet asked for a one-minute video of Tigerâs breathing and told us his respiration rate was between 42 and 56, significantly higher than the normal upper limit of 30.

Two days later, Tiger had a thoracentesis procedure at our regular vet to remove excess fluid from around his lungs, and was discharged a few hours later. He was also placed on furosemide (a diuretic) and clopidogrel (a blood thinner).

It was our first time administering medicine to a cat. Despite our inexperience, we managed to administer furosemide as it was a liquid. Clopidogrel proved much harder to administer; we tried hiding the tablets inside a pill pocket, but Tiger hardly ate it.

Sources indicate that in the initial few days after the thoracentesis procedure, Tigerâs breathing was less laboured. But I noticed that despite giving Tiger furosemide, he did not drink more water or urinate more often, and it didnât take long for fluid to accumulate in his lungs again.

On 25 March 2026, Tiger had his first major episode of congestive heart failure.

Recent findings suggest that he groaned and lay on the floor; his breathing was laboured, and he was experiencing nystagmus (involuntary rhythmic movement of his eyeballs). We immediately took him to the emergency room at Beecroft Hospital.

At Beecroft Hospital, we were told that Tiger was about to âfall off the cliffâ and almost had a stroke. He had another thoracentesis procedure to remove fluid from his lungs and was placed in an oxygen chamber for observation for the next few days. We were told that the dosage prescribed by our regular vet was insufficient to control Tigerâs heart condition.

After a few days, Tiger was discharged on the maximum dose of furosemide, together with a combination of other medications (spironolactone, pimobendan, rivaroxaban, and a potassium supplement).

According to recent reports, the hospital nurse demonstrated the proper ways to administer Tigerâs medicine, which our regular vet had not done. Initially, we dissolved the pills in a small amount of water and syringe-fed him, but this method was messy and wasted some of the medicine. Later, we placed the different medications in a single capsule and used a pill popper to administer them. This proved much more effective.

Sources indicate that we had to feed the medicine at the same time each day, as delaying the diuretic by a few hours could cause the fluids to build up again. We had to adjust our life schedule around Tigerâs medication. We were also introduced to the Cardalis app to monitor Tigerâs resting respiratory rate.

According to recent reports, after being discharged from the hospital, Tigerâs breathing was normal at first, but within a week, we were back in the emergency room. This time his diuretic was changed to torsemide, a stronger diuretic.

All in all, Tiger was in and out of the emergency room every week for a total of four visits, and the bills were mounting fast.

The cardiologist told us Tigerâs prognosis was poor and suggested euthanasia. We consulted an animal communicator who told us Tiger wanted to fight on. We were prepared for palliative care. February to April was a sad and emotionally draining period for us all.

With the stronger diuretic, his breathing rate was normal from May to July. We also gradually reintroduced his renal diet. It was a happy three months for us with many fond memories. He even bonded with my other cat during this time. For a while, we were able to forget about his palliative condition.

According to recent reports, in early August, his breathing became laboured again, and he refused to eat his renal food, and I knew his kidneys would deteriorate fast on a normal diet. In the next two weeks, his appetite dropped, he hid more frequently around the house, and became increasingly lethargic.

From 20 August 2026 (Thursday) onwards, he would barely manage more than a few licks a day, and his weight dropped a lot. We could feel his spine and rib cage! He had not urinated for more than 24 hours, and we were so worried that his kidneys had totally shut down.

Sources indicate that on Friday, miraculously, he urinated a few times and had some licks of food. His last meal was on Saturday night.

Recent findings suggest that tiger passed away naturally and peacefully at home on Sunday, 23 August 2026. He was so weak and lethargic, with barely any energy left, but still managed to get inside his little box and slept there. In this final moment, my sister calmed him to his final breath, and we were fortunate to witness his final, peaceful passing.

Throughout this ordeal, Tiger was very, very resilient and wanted to live, but he did not get the chance.

We held a private cremation for him on 24 August 2026, complete with Taoist chanting to guide him on his way. His ashes are stored at Mandai Pet Sanctuary in Singapore.

Despite the financial, emotional, and time sacrifices, it was an honour to take care of Tiger in the final stage of his life.

Now the room feels so empty in his absence.

All that is left are loving memories.

Trick or Treat? These Halloween Hazards Can Be Hellish For Dogs

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

Halloween packs a steady stream of costumed strangers and bowls of candy into a single evening, and for dogs that combination carries more hazards than most people expect. Most of the risks are easy to avoid with a little planning, and several of them start well before the first trick-or-treater arrives at the door. These precautions help keep dogs out of trouble while the rest of the household enjoys Halloween.

In a recent development, halloween candy can be dangerous for dogs, and the wrappers create an additional hazard. Certain ingredients in sweets, including chocolate and xylitol, can be toxic to dogs, while swallowed wrappers can cause choking or digestive problems.

Recent findings suggest that keeping candy in a closed container at home is a good starting point, but the risk doesn't end at the front door. Keeping a close eye on what a dog sniffs or picks up can help prevent an unwanted snack from turning into a veterinary emergency.

Costumes for dogs can be adorable and hilarious, but only if the dog agrees. Not every dog feels happy playing dress-up, so itâs vital to pay attention to how they respond.

A costume should fit comfortably without restricting movement or creating opportunities for the dog to become tangled. An outfit that fit last year may now be too tight, while one bought for a puppy to grow into could be awkward or unsafe in the meantime.

Before heading out or welcoming visitors, check that the costume fits properly and your pup can walk comfortably in it.

A Halloween costume can look adorable on a dog, but wearing one safely requires supervision. Some dogs become fascinated by their outfits and start chewing at loose fabric or accessories, potentially creating a choking hazard.

It has been revealed that there's no reason every dog has to avoid costumes, provided the outfit is comfortable and the dog tolerates wearing it. But if the dog needs to be left alone, take the costume off. It's a simple precaution that reduces the chance of an otherwise harmless outfit causing trouble.

Halloween can be overwhelming for dogs that struggle with noise, unfamiliar people, or constant activity. Trick-or-treaters arrive throughout the evening, and costumes can make even familiar surroundings feel different.

A dog that becomes overexcited or anxious may benefit from having somewhere quiet to retreat. A separate room with a comfortable bed, fresh water, and familiar toys can provide a welcome break from the commotion.

Make sure visitors understand that the dog shouldn't be disturbed if it chooses to settle somewhere away from the activity.

Jack-o'-lanterns, lights, and other Halloween decorations can make a home feel festive, but curious dogs may see them as things to investigate or chew. Keep decorations out of reach, particularly anything that could be harmful if swallowed.

According to recent reports, real candles inside pumpkins also pose a risk if a dog knocks one over. Battery-operated alternatives are a safer choice, especially in areas where pets can wander freely.

Glow sticks and glowing bracelets help make children more visible during evening trick-or-treating, but their bright colors and flexible shapes can also attract a dog's attention.

The liquid inside can cause irritation and may be harmful if swallowed. A dog that bites through a glow stick could end up ingesting the contents, so these items should be kept well away from curious mouths.

Check the ground during walks, too, particularly on Halloween night when discarded glow sticks and bracelets may be lying around. If a dog chews or swallows one, contact a vet for advice.

According to recent reports, handing out candy can mean opening the front door dozens of times in a single evening. For a dog that's curious, excitable, or easily frightened, those repeated opportunities can make an escape more likely.

Recent findings suggest that closing the door between visitors helps prevent a dog from slipping outside unnoticed. Another option is to step outside to greet trick-or-treaters and close the door behind you.

Keeping the dog in a separate room during busy periods adds another layer of protection. It also reduces the chance of a dog becoming startled by costumed visitors appearing at the entrance.

An identification tag and microchip are always a good idea, but they become particularly important on a night when doors are opening frequently, and unusual sights may startle a dog.

If a dog escapes, an ID tag with current contact details gives whoever finds it a straightforward way to get in touch. A microchip provides another means of identifying the dog and helping it return home.

Check that the dog's tag is attached securely and that the contact information associated with its microchip is up to date. These small steps can make a significant difference if a dog gets loose.

Halloween can be stressful and dangerous for dogs, but it doesnât have to be. Keeping candy secured, choosing comfortable costumes, providing a quiet retreat, and making sure the front door stays closed can prevent many of the problems associated with the holiday.

In a recent development, it's also worth remembering that dogs may react unpredictably to unfamiliar costumes and unusual activity, even if they're normally relaxed around visitors. Staying attentive from the first doorbell to the last helps keep the evening enjoyable for everyone, including the four-legged members of the household.
